Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 1–2:

Makkiyya (Meccan), except His words "And the poets..." to the end of the surah. It has two hundred and twenty-seven verses. In another narration, it has two hundred and twenty-six verses [it was revealed after al-Waqi'a].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ta Sin Mim, with the alif pronounced emphatically and inclined (imala), and the nun both made clear (izhar) and assimilated (idgham).

﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾: its miraculousness is manifest, and its being from Allah is sound. By "the Book" is meant either the surah or the Qur'an. The meaning: the verses of this composition are made of the letters that are spread out; ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾.

Al-Bakhʿ (البخع): to cut the slaughter so deep that it reaches the bakhaa (البخاع), with the bāʾ, which is a vein running along the inside of the spine; and that is the furthest limit of slaughtering. Laʿalla (لعل) here expresses concern (al-ishfaq), meaning: "Be concerned for yourself lest you kill yourself out of grief over what has escaped you of your people's acceptance of Islam" (أَلَّا يَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ) — that is, lest they not believe; or on account of their refusal to believe; or for fear that they will not believe. And it is related from Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read it as bākhiʿun nafsaka with the genitive construction (ʿalā al-iḍāfa).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verse 4:

He means: a sign compelling belief and restricted to it. "Fa-zallat" (and so they remain) is coordinated with the conditional response, which is "nunazzil" (We would send down), for if it were said "anzalnā" (We sent down), it would be correct. Its parallel is "fa-asaddaqa wa-akun" (so that I may give charity and be among the righteous), as if it were said "asaddaq" (I would give charity). It has also been recited: "law shi'nā la-anzalnā" (if We willed, We would have sent down).

And it has been recited: "fa-tazall a'nāquhum" (so their necks would remain). If you ask: how is it valid for "khāḍi'īn" (humbled) to come as a predicate of "a'nāq" (necks)? I say: the original wording is "fa-ẓallū lahā khāḍi'īn" (so they would remain humbled before it), and "al-a'nāq" (the necks) was inserted to indicate the place of humbling, and the speech was left in its original form, like his saying: "dhahabat ahl al-Yamāma" (the people of al-Yamāma went), as if "al-ahl" (the people) were not mentioned. Or, since the necks were described with humbling, which belongs to rational beings, it was said "khāḍi'īn," like His saying, exalted is He, "lī sājidīn" (prostrating to me). It was also said that "a'nāq al-nās" (the necks of the people) means their leaders and foremost ones, who were likened to necks, just as they were called "al-ru'ūs" (the heads), "al-nawāṣī" (the forelocks), and "al-ṣudūr" (the chests). He said:

"fī maḥfilin min nawāṣī al-nāsi mashhūdi" [[The explanation of this evidence was given earlier in the second volume, page 428; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

It was also said: groups of people. It is said: "jā'anā 'unqun min al-nās" (a band of people came to us), meaning a group of them. It has also been recited: "fa-ẓallat a'nāquhum lahā khāḍi'a." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: this verse was revealed concerning us and concerning the Banu Umayya. He said: "The dominion will be ours over them, and their necks will be humbled to us after difficulty, and humiliation will overtake them after honour."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 5–6:

Meaning: Whenever Allah renews for them a reminder through His revelation, admonishing and warning, they only renew their turning away from it and their disbelief in it. If you ask: How are the expressions varied while the purpose is one, namely turning away (i'rad), denial (takdhib), and mockery (istihza')? I answer: They are varied only because the aims differ, as if it were said: When they turned away from the Reminder, they had denied it; and when they denied it, its worth became light in their eyes, and it became a target for mockery and derision. This is because whoever is receptive to the truth and turns towards it will inevitably affirm it and will not be suspected of denying it. And whoever affirms it will hold it in honour. ﴿So there will certainly come to them the news﴾: this is a threat to them and a warning that they will know, when the punishment of Allah touches them on the day of Badr or on the Day of Resurrection, what the thing was that they used to mock, namely the Qur'an; and its tidings and its circumstances, which were hidden from them, will come to them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 7–9:

He described the pair (zawj), meaning the kind of plant, as "generous" (karim). The word karim (generous, noble) describes anything that is pleasing and praiseworthy in its own category. One says "a noble face" (wajh karim) when it is pleasing in its beauty and comeliness, and "a noble book" (kitab karim) when it is pleasing in its meanings and benefits. The poet said:

*Until he cleaves the ranks with his nobility*
*Did you see our day and the day of Banu al-Taym?*
*When the dust of its battle clung to its blood...*

*When they saw that their day was dense (ashabb),*
*They tightened their girdles over their pain.*

*They are like lions in their thicket (arin),*
*And we are like the night that surges in its darkness (qatm).*

*They do not abandon their neighbour at dawn*
*Until the sandal-strap slips from his foot.*

*And their horseman does not shrink from the encounter*
*Until he cleaves the ranks with his nobility.*

It is for a man of Himyar. Min (in the line "min ra'a") is interrogative. Al-sayq and al-sayqa (with a kasra) are dust and earth. Al-ashabb (on the pattern of hadhar) is that which has much noise and confusion, and it is also applied to a place whose trees are intertwined. Al-hayzum is the chest. Al-arin is the thicket where the lion lives.

Jash means rose and approached. Al-qatm means dust, blackness and darkness. It is also transmitted as fi ghashmihi, with a ghayn, and the meaning is the same: "they do not abandon" means they do not forsake or leave behind. Al-shiraak is the strap of the sandal. "Wa la yakhaym" means he does not flinch from the encounter. Al-yawm means the time or the event. The attribution of the dust and the blood to the day is because they occur in it. Describing the day as abounding in cries and confusion is because these things take place in it. Tightening the girdles over pain is a metonymy (kinaya) for fortitude and patience. He compared them to lions in their courage, and he compared their people to the night in its encompassing and its subjugation of others. Then he said: they do not abandon their ally at the dawn of terror until he is left alone in war. The slipping of the sandal-strap is a metonymy for this. Their horseman does not shrink from the encounter. The word "min karimihi" is in the accusative by dropping the preposition (naz' al-khafid), and it has been said that it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu). Until he cleaves the ranks of battle and enters them with his nobility, meaning his courage and boldness, because nobility in every category is according to that category. The first "hatta" is the limit of the negated, and the second is the limit of the negation. It is permissible that the second "hatta" be inceptive (ibtida'iyya), with the verb after it in the nominative as a resumption (isti'naf). This is more eloquent in praise. Then, praising their enemy is praise of them.

That is: from the fact that he is pleasing in his courage and might. The generous plant is the one that is pleasing in the benefits connected with it.

﴿Indeed, in the growing of those kinds there is surely a sign﴾ that the One who brought them forth is able to give life to the dead, and God knows that most of them are sealed upon their hearts, and their faith is not to be hoped for. ﴿And indeed your Lord, He is the Mighty﴾ in His vengeance against the disbelievers, ﴿the Merciful﴾ to whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds.

If you say: what is the meaning of combining "kam" and "kull"? Had it been said, "How many noble pairs have We caused to grow therein?" [The saying "How many noble pairs have We caused to grow therein" has perhaps a lacuna after it, its intended form being "was upright". (ʿ)] You say: "kull" indicates the encompassing of the pairs of plants in detail, and "kam" indicates that this encompassed thing is abundant and exceedingly numerous. [Mahmud said: "If you say: what is the benefit of combining kull and kam? He answered that kull is used for the encompassing of the pairs of plants, and kam indicates that what is encompassed is abundant and exceedingly numerous." Ahmad said: according to this, the intended abundance is of kinds. But the apparent meaning is that the intended abundance is of the individual pairs and the cattle. This is shown by the fact that if you removed "kull" and said, "Look at the earth, how many of such-and-such kind God has caused to grow in it," you would be alluding to the individual members of that specified kind. When you add "kull", by repeating it you have expressed the individuals of every kind, not the individuals of one specified kind. And God knows best.] This is the meaning of combining them, and by it He draws attention to the perfection of His power.

If you say: what is the meaning of describing the pair as "noble"? You say it may bear two meanings. One: that plants are of two kinds, beneficial and harmful, so He mentioned the abundance of what He has caused to grow on earth from all kinds of beneficial plants, and left out mention of the harmful. Two: that it includes all plants, both their beneficial and harmful kinds, and describes them all as noble, and it draws attention to the fact that He has not caused anything to grow except that there is in it a benefit, because the Wise does not do an act except for a sound purpose and a profound wisdom, even if the heedless are unaware of it and the intelligent have not reached knowledge of it.

If you say: when He mentioned the pairs and indicated them by the two words of abundance and encompassing, and they are such that none can count them except the Knower of the Unseen, how did He say ﴿Indeed in that is surely a sign﴾ and not say "signs"? You say there are two possibilities: that it refers to the verbal noun of "We caused to grow", so that it is as if He said, "Indeed in the growing there is surely a sign, what a sign!" And that it means: in each one of those pairs there is a sign. There have been precedents for this aspect before.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verse 10–11:

He recorded their wrongdoing against them by placing "the wrongdoing people" first, and then attached "Pharaoh's people" to them in apposition (ʿatf al-bayan), as if the meaning of "the wrongdoing people" and its explanation were "the people of Pharaoh." They are two expressions that alternate over one and the same meaning: if he wished to mention them, he described them as "the wrongdoing people," and if he wished, he described them as "the people of Pharaoh." They deserved this designation from two aspects: from the aspect of their wronging themselves through disbelief and wickedness, and from the aspect of their wronging the Children of Israel by enslaving them.

It was read: ﴿ألا يتقون﴾ with a kasra on the nun (ʾalā yattaqūn), meaning: ﴿ألا يتقونني﴾ ("will they not fear Me"), so the nun was dropped because of the meeting of two nuns, and the yāʾ was dropped as being sufficed by the kasra.

If you say: With what is his saying ﴿ألا يتقون﴾ connected? I say: It is a resumed statement, which He, may He be exalted, followed with His sending of him to them as a warner and His recording of their wrongdoing, expressing wonder to Moses at their condition, which was grievous in wrongdoing and oppression, and at their sense of security regarding consequences, and the scarcity of their fear and caution regarding the days of Allah. It is also possible that ﴿لا يتقون﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿الظالمين﴾, meaning: they wrong while not being mindful of Allah and His punishment, so the interrogative hamza of denial (hamzat al-inkar) was placed before the circumstantial clause.

As for the one who read ﴿ألا تتقون﴾ in the second person (khiṭāb), it is by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person) toward them, confronting them and striking their faces with denial and anger against them, as you see one who complains about someone who committed a crime to a close associate while the criminal is present: when he launches into the complaint and his temperament heats up [[The phrase "wa-harra mizājahu" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: ḥarra yaḥurru ḥarran wa-ḥarāratan wa-ḥarūran. (ʿ)]] and his anger flares, he cuts off speaking to his companion, turns to the criminal, rebukes him and reproaches him, and says to him: "Do you not fear Allah? Are you not ashamed before people?" If you say: What is the benefit of this iltifat, when the address is with Moses, peace be upon him, at the time of intimate conversation, and the one turned to them is absent and unaware? I say: Applying that to the speech addressed to those to whom he was sent has the same effect as applying it in their presence and delivering it to their ears, because he is their conveyor, their admonisher, and their publicizer among people, and in it there is a subtle kindness and an incitement to increase piety. How many a verse was revealed about disbelievers, yet it contains the greatest share for the believers, by reflecting on it and taking a lesson from its context.

And in ﴿ألا يتقون﴾ with the yāʾ and a kasra on the nun there is another possibility, namely that the meaning is: ﴿ألا يا ناس اتقون﴾ ("O people, fear Me"), like His saying ﴿ألا يسجدوا﴾ ("that they should not prostrate").

As for the one who read ﴿ألا تتقون﴾ in the second person (khiṭāb), it is by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person) toward them, confronting them and striking their faces with denial and anger against them, as you see one who complains about someone who committed a crime to a close associate while the criminal is present: when he launches into the complaint and his temperament heats up [[The phrase "wa-harra mizājahu" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: ḥarra yaḥurru ḥarran wa-ḥarāratan wa-ḥarūran. (ʿ)]] and his anger flares, he cuts off speaking to his companion, turns to the criminal, rebukes him and reproaches him, and says to him: "Do you not fear Allah? Are you not ashamed before people?" If you say: What is the benefit of this iltifat, when the address is with Moses, peace be upon him, at the time of intimate conversation, and the one turned to them is absent and unaware? I say: Applying that to the speech addressed to those to whom he was sent has the same effect as applying it in their presence and delivering it to their ears, because he is their conveyor, their admonisher, and their publicizer among people, and in it there is a subtle kindness and an incitement to increase piety. How many a verse was revealed about disbelievers, yet it contains the greatest share for the believers, by reflecting on it and taking a lesson from its context.

And in ﴿ألا يتقون﴾ with the yāʾ and a kasra on the nun there is another possibility, namely that the meaning is: ﴿ألا يا ناس اتقون﴾ ("O people, fear Me"), like His saying ﴿ألا يسجدوا﴾ ("that they should not prostrate").

Verse-by-verse, "wa-yadiqu wa-yanṭaliq" (and my chest tightens and my tongue does not speak freely): read in the nominative, they are coordinated with the predicate of inna (indeed), and in the accusative, they are coordinated with the complement of an (that).

The difference between them in meaning: the nominative indicates that there are three causes (ʿilal) of fear: fear of being denied, tightness of the chest, and the impossibility of the tongue's free movement. The accusative indicates that his fear is connected to these three things. If you say: in the accusative, the fear is linked to the three matters, and among them is the negation of the tongue's free movement; but the reality of fear is only a distress that befalls a person over a matter that will happen, and that (the impediment) was already existing, so how is it permissible to link the fear to it? I answer: the fear has been linked to their denial and to what results for him from it of tightness of the chest, and the impediment in the tongue was in addition to what he already had; moreover, that impediment which he had has disappeared through his call (to Allah). It was said: a small remnant of it remained.

If you say: this excuse of yours is refuted by the nominative, because the meaning is: "I fear, my chest is tight, and my tongue is not free." I answer: it is permissible that this (state) was before the call and its acceptance; it is permissible that he means the small amount that remained with him; and it is permissible that it was not with the untying of the knot of his tongue, (as he was) among the eloquent, the orators (muṣaqqaʿūn, "al-faṣīḥ al-muṣāqiʿ") who have been given fluency of tongues and breadth of speech. Harun was of that quality, so he wished to be paired with him. What indicates this is His saying, exalted is He: "My brother Harun is more eloquent than me in tongue" (Qur'an 28:34).

The meaning of "fa-arsil ila Harun" (so send to Harun): send Gabriel to him, make him a prophet, and strengthen me with him (wa-āzirnī bihi, "to support, help"), and tighten my arm through him. This is a concise statement. He has expanded on it in another place. He has excelled in brevity when he said "fa-arsil ila Harun," bringing in something that includes the meaning of making him a prophet. A similar example of shortening what is long, and of excellence, is His saying, exalted is He: "So We said: Go to the people who denied Our signs, then We destroyed them with destruction" (Qur'an 25:36), where He confined Himself to mentioning the two ends of the story, its beginning and its end, which are the warning and the destruction, and by mentioning them He indicated the purpose of the whole long story, namely that they were a people who denied the signs of Allah, so Allah willed to establish the proof against them, sent two messengers to them, they denied them, and so He destroyed them.

If you say: how was it fitting for Musa (peace be upon him) that Allah commanded him with a matter and he did not receive it with hearing and obedience without hesitation and clinging to causes, while he knew that Allah was behind him? I answer: he complied and accepted, but he asked his Lord that He strengthen him with his brother so that the two of them might cooperate in carrying out His command and conveying His message. So before his request he prepared his excuse for what he asked, then he asked after that; and preparing an excuse in asking for a helper to carry out a command is not hesitation in complying with the command, nor an pretext in it, and the request for help is sufficient proof of acceptance, not of pretext.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verse 14:

He intended by the sin: his killing of the Copt. It was also said: he was a baker of Pharaoh, whose name was Fatun. The meaning is: "And they have a claim against me for a sin, which is retaliation for that killing [[His saying "which is retaliation for that killing" perhaps should read "the one killed" (al-qatil). (Ghayn)]], so I fear they will kill me for it," where the genitive complement has been omitted. Or he called the consequence of the sin a sin, just as the recompense of an evil deed is called an evil deed. If you say: you have refused to make those three into reasons, and you made them a preface to an excuse for what he sought, so what is your view of this fourth one? I say: this is a seeking of protection against the anticipated calamity, and a fear of being killed before discharging the message, so how could it be an pretext? The proof of this is what came after it of the word of restraint (kallā), and the promise of protection and deliverance.

Allah combined both responses in His words ﴿Nay; go, both of you﴾, because [Moses] asked Him to repel their harm, so He promised him protection by restraining them from fear. He also asked for support through his brother, so He answered him with ﴿go﴾, meaning: go, you and the one you asked for, who is Harun (Aaron). If you ask, "What is ﴿go﴾ conjoined to?" I say: it is conjoined to the verb implied by ﴿Nay﴾, as if it were said: "Desist, O Moses, from what you suppose, and go, you and Harun." His words ﴿with you, listening﴾ are a figurative expression (majaz, a meaning other than the literal). He intends: "I am for you both and against your enemy, like a helper and supporter for you against him when he is present and hears what passes between you and him. So I will make you prevail, overcome him, break his power over you, and subdue him."

It is permissible for the two words to be predicates of inna (indeed), or for mustami'un (listening) to be a predicate and ma'akum (with you) to be a dependent phrase. If you ask, "Why did you make mustami'un a counterpart to ma'akum in being figurative, when Allah is literally described as Sami' (All-Hearing) and Sami' (Hearer)?" I say: He is not literally described as mustami' (one who listens intently), because istima' (listening) takes the place of isgha' (attentive hearing), and istima' relates to sam' (hearing) as nazar (looking) relates to ru'ya (seeing). From this is His saying: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened, and said: Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾. It is also said: "He listened to his speech" and "He heard his speech", meaning: he attended to it and perceived it with the sense of hearing.

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): [[I have not found this wording. What is preserved is "molten lead (al-anak) is poured into his ears," meaning lead. Ibn al-Athir mentioned it in al-Nihaya with the wording "al-burm al-dam" [i.e., "blood"?], and said: it is kohl melted. I say: Ibn al-Athir took it only from al-Fa'iq, which goes back to al-Zamakhshari.]] "Whoever listens to the talk of a people who dislike it, al-burm will be poured into his ears." [[On "al-burm will be poured into his ears": in al-Sihah, "al-burm" is the fruit of the acacia tree. (ʿ)]]

If you ask, "Why did he not make the messenger dual, as in His words ﴿We are both messengers of your Lord﴾?" I say: rasul (messenger) can mean "one sent" and can mean "a message." When it means "one sent," it must be made dual. Here it means "message," so it is permissible to treat it, when used as a description, uniformly for singular, dual, and plural, as is done with the descriptive use of verbal nouns, such as sawm (fasting) and zawr (falsehood). A poet said:

*Convey me to her, for the best of messengers [i.e., of messages] is the one most knowing of the paths of news.*

So he made it plural [a'lamuhum, "most knowing of them"]. The evidence for rasul meaning "message" is the line:

*The slanderers have lied: I did not utter a secret among them, nor did I send them with a messenger.*

[[Ascribed to Kuthayyir, the companion of 'Azza:

*I swear by the Lord of the dancing mounts going to Mina, through the midst of the crowd, each with a halter on its neck being pulled:*
*The slanderers have lied: I did not utter a secret among them, nor did I send them with a messenger.*
*So do not hasten, O 'Azza, to be deceived by advice, whether the slanderers brought it or with calamities.*

"Al-raqisat" are the riding beasts going to Mina for the pilgrimage; "khilal al-mala'" means "amid the people"; "al-jadil" is the halter on its neck which he pulls. "Al-washi" is one who embellishes speech, disguises it, mixes truth with falsehood, and distorts words from their places. "Ma" is negative: I did not utter a secret among them, nor did I send them to anyone with a messenger, meaning a message, since it is originally a verbal noun. It may also refer to the one sent, which is what appears in one version: "nor did I correspond with them by a messenger," meaning I did not confide the secret to them nor send a messenger to them with it. This version better matches the antithesis. It is possible that arsaltahum means arsaltu ilayhim (I sent to them). The original is "O 'Azza," which was shortened by dropping the taa'. "An tanfahimi" means "in that you understand" or "for you to understand." "Bi-nasihin" means: is it by sincere advice that the slanderers came to you, or by calamities? "Hubul" is the plural of hibl, meaning a great calamity, and there is no greater calamity than lying.]] It is also permissible that the word be singular, because their ruling is one, since they support each other and agree on one law, and their unity in this, and their brotherhood, made them a single authority, as if they were one messenger. Or it is meant that each of them is ﴿an arsil﴾ (send), where arsil means ay arsil (that is, "send"), because rasul includes the meaning of irsal (sending). One says: "I sent to you that you should do such-and-such," because irsal contains the meaning of speech, as in calling out, writing, and similar things. The meaning of this irsal is release and letting go, like your saying: "Release the falcon," meaning: let them go with us to Palestine, which was their dwelling place.

It is reported that they went to the gate of Pharaoh and were not admitted for a year, until the doorkeeper said: "Here is a man who claims to be a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him." So they delivered the message. Moses was recognized, and Pharaoh said to him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ There is an omission here: they came to Pharaoh and told him this, because it was known and not doubtful.

This kind of abridgment is common in the revelation. Al-walid means a young child, because of his recent birth. In a report from Abu 'Amr, the reading is "min 'umrika" (from your life), with the mim sukun (unvocalized). ﴿Years﴾: it is said he stayed among them for thirty years.

It is also said that he struck the Copt when he was twelve years old, and fled from them afterward. Allah knows best the soundness of this.

It is reported from al-Sha'bi: "fa'latika" with a kasra, which refers to the killing of the Copt, because he killed him with a blow, which is a kind of killing. But "fa'lah" (with a fatha) refers to a single blow. [Al-Zamakhshari said:] He enumerated His favor upon him, namely his upbringing and bringing him to the age of manhood, and reproached him for what happened at his hand, namely the killing of his servant, and made it appear monstrous. [Quoting al-Zamakhshari in the text:] "He enumerated His favor upon him and reproached him for what happened at his hands, the killing of his servant, and made it appear monstrous to him by saying: ﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you were of the disbelievers﴾." Ahmad [al-Muntasif] said: The way it is made monstrous is that by stating it in vague and ambiguous terms, it signals that its heinousness is such that it can only be mentioned by allusion. A similar case of magnification through vagueness is His words: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea what covered them﴾, ﴿when there covers the lote-tree what covers it﴾, and ﴿then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. Similar examples are many, and Allah knows best.

His words ﴿and you were of the disbelievers﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, meaning: you killed him while being among the disbelievers in My favor. Or it means: you were at that time among those who will be called disbelievers at the Hour, and he was slandered or his affair was misunderstood, because he was living among them under taqiyya (dissimulation), for Allah protects from every grave sin, and from some minor sins, whoever He wills to make a prophet, so what of disbelief?

It is also permissible that His words ﴿and you were of the disbelievers﴾ be a judgment against him that he is among those who disbelieve in favors. Whoever's habit is ingratitude toward favors, for him killing the close associates of his benefactor is not strange. Or it means he is among those who disbelieve in Pharaoh and his divinity. Or he was among those who were disbelievers in their religion, for they had gods that they worshipped. This is witnessed by His words: ﴿and abandon you and your gods﴾. It was also read as "ilahatak" (your goddess).

Moses answered him that that deed had occurred from him when he was ﴿of the astray﴾, meaning: the ignorant. The reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "min al-jahilin" (of the ignorant), is explanatory. The meaning is: among those who do the deed of people of ignorance and foolishness, as Joseph said to his brothers: ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant?﴾ Or it means "those who err," like one who kills by mistake without intending to kill. Or it means "those who go astray from the right course."

Or it means "the forgetful," from His words: ﴿lest one of them err and the other remind her﴾. Pharaoh lied and rejected the description of disbelief from himself, and cleared his own reputation by putting "the astray" in place of "the disbelievers," out of respect for the one who was nominated for prophethood, from that description. Then he returned to his favor upon him by upbringing, and nullified it at its root and uprooted it from its origin, and refused to name his favor anything but a calamity. He made clear that the real nature of his favor upon him was the enslavement of the Children of Israel, because their enslavement and the intent behind slaughtering their sons was the cause of his being taken in and raised. So it is as if he had favored him by enslaving his people, if the matter is investigated. Their enslavement means: humiliating them and making them slaves. It is said: "I enslaved the man and made him a slave," when one takes him as a slave. [Poem:]

*Why do my people enslave me, when among them there are many camels and servants, whatever they wish?*

["ʿalam" is a rhetorical question of denial about the cause, meaning: for what? "A'badtu al-rajul" and "ʿabadtuhu" mean taking him as a slave. "Al-aba'ir" is the plural of ba'ir, applied to male and female camels. "Al-ʿabd" is pluralized as ʿabdan (with kasra or damma), ʿabdi (with doubled dal, short and long), ma'buda, 'ibad, a'bud, 'ubayd, and 'abd (with two dammas or two fathas). He says: "For what reason do they take me as a slave, when camels and slaves have multiplied among them because of me? Let them take from them whatever they wish." "Whatever they wish" is either a substitute for "camels" or stands in place of the verbal noun for "multiplied," indicating abundance. In this situation there is mockery of them and an indication of their foolishness. It is also possible that the meaning is: while some of them are like camels and some are slaves, let them be content with some of them instead of me. It was said that the restriction to this state is because it is what moved them to be arrogant toward him.]

If you ask, "The response is also the condition, while the speech was a reply to Pharaoh. How, then, did it become a condition?" I say: Pharaoh's words ﴿you did your deed﴾ contain the meaning: you rewarded my favor with what you did. Moses said to him: "Yes, I did it, rewarding you," accepting his statement, because his favor was in his view worthy of being repaid with such a reward.

If you ask, "Why did he make the pronoun plural in ﴿minkum﴾ (from you) and ﴿khiftukum﴾ (I feared you), while making it singular in ﴿ni'matuha﴾ (its favor) and ﴿'abbadta﴾ (you enslaved)?" I say: the fear and the flight were not from him alone, but from him and his chiefs who conspired to kill him, as shown by His words: ﴿Indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾. As for the favor, it was from him alone, and likewise the enslavement.

If you ask, "What does ﴿that﴾ (tilka) refer to, and what is the grammatical position of ﴿an 'abbadta﴾ (that you enslaved)?" I say: tilka refers to a hideous, vague trait, which is not known until it is explained. The position of ﴿an 'abbadta﴾ is in the nominative as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) of tilka. Its parallel is His words: ﴿And We decreed to him that matter, that the root of these is cut off﴾. The meaning is: your enslavement of the Children of Israel is a favor you bestow upon me. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that ﴿an﴾ be in the accusative position, meaning: it became a favor upon me only because you enslaved the Children of Israel. That is, had you not done that, my family would have taken care of me and would not have thrown me into the river.

[[Editor's note: al-Zamakhshari's phrase "wa-istasalahu min sanikhihi" appears in the edition with a variant; in al-Sihah, "al-sanakh" means family, and "sanakha al-'ilm sunukh" means it became firmly established, while "sanakha al-dahr" (with kasra) is a dialect form of "zanakha," meaning it became corrupted and its smell changed. One says: "a house with a stench and a stink." (ʿ)]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verse 23:

When his gatekeeper told him that there was here one who claimed to be a messenger of the Lord of the worlds, he said to him upon his entry: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ He meant: what is the Lord of the worlds? This question admits of no escape: either he meant by it, "What is He among the things that have been witnessed and whose genera are known?" and so he [Moses] answered him with what is inferred of Him from His particular acts, to make him know that He is not any of the things that have been witnessed and known, of bodies and accidents, and that He is a thing unlike all things: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. Or he meant by it: "What is He in absolute terms?", seeking out His particular reality, what it is. So [Moses] answered him that the way to Him, and what suffices for knowing Him, is knowing His affirmation through His attributes, inferring that from His particular acts. As for searching out His particular reality, which lies beyond the natural disposition of minds, it is a search for what has no way to it, and the one who asks about it is a obstinate person, not one seeking the truth. What befits Pharaoh's condition and what the speech indicates is:

that this question of his was a denial that there could be a Lord of the worlds other than himself, on account of his claim to divinity. So when Moses answered with what he answered, his people marvelled at his answer, in that he attributed lordship to other than him. Then, when he [Moses] repeated the affirmation of his statement, [Pharaoh] turned to his people and mocked him,[[His saying "wa-tanaza bihi" means: he mocked him and became incensed, i.e., his chest was inflamed with rage. Stated in al-Sihah. (Gloss)]] calling him their messenger. When he [Moses] repeated it a third time with another affirmation, he grew furious and became enraged, and said: ﴿If you take a god other than me...﴾. This indicates the soundness of this last interpretation.

**Question:** How can it be said ﴿وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ ("and what is between them") in the dual, when the thing referred to is plural?

**Answer:** I mean "and what is between the two kinds." He treated the pronoun as he would treat a noun, as in the poet's words:

[[In the battle, two camels... He collected one year's zakat (*'iqal*), leaving us not a single *sabad*. So how would it be if 'Amr had collected two years' *'iqal*?

Then the people would have been ruined or destroyed, and at their dispersal in battle they would not have found two camels.

*Al-sa'i*: the one appointed to collect zakat. *Al-'iqal*: the zakat of one year, and here it means the year itself, because it functions as an adverbial of time. *Al-sabad*: a small amount. It is said, "He has no *sabad* and no *labad*," meaning he has neither little nor much. Al-Asma'i said: the first (*sabad*) is from hair, and the second (*labad*) is from wool. *Al-awbad*: the plural of *wabad* (with two fathas), whose original meaning is narrowness of living and bad condition; it is used as an adjective for emphasis. He made "camels" dual in the sense of two kinds of them, or two groups of them, even if they are of one kind. He says: he collected the zakat of one year, and so he wronged us and left us not a small part of our wealth. How, then, would our situation be if he had collected for two years? Mentioning 'Amr after his pronoun has already been used carries a kind of awe-inspiring effect. It may also be from the grammatical construction called *tanazu'* (contention between two verbs for one noun): the noun could be the subject of the first verb, while the second verb's subject is its pronoun. The phrase "then the people would have..." (*li-asbaha*) is governed by an omitted clause, meaning: if he had collected two years' zakat, the people would have perished from poverty, and at their dispersal in war they would not have found two kinds of camels, one for each group, so the conduct of military campaigns would be disrupted, since the enemy might be engaged on two fronts, or rather on many fronts, requiring two camels or even more.]]

**Question:** What is the meaning of ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُوقِنِينَ﴾ ("if you are certain"), and how does it relate to Pharaoh and his chiefs, who were not certain?

**Answer:** The meaning is: if there is hope that you will attain the certainty that correct reflection leads to, then this answer benefits you; otherwise it will not benefit you.

Or: if you are certain of anything at all, then this is the most fitting thing for you to be certain of, because it is so evident and its proof so clear.

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 25–28:

"He said to those around him: Do you not hear?" [This is the verse's own wording.] Fa-in qulta: "And who were those around him?" Qultu: "The nobles of his people." It was said: they were five hundred men, wearing bracelets, for bracelets were reserved for kings.

Fa-in qulta: The mention of the heavens and the earth and what is between them has already encompassed all created beings, so what is the meaning of mentioning them, and their fathers after that, and mentioning the East and the West? Qultu: He first generalised, then specified from the general, for clarification, themselves and their fathers. For the nearest thing a rational person contemplates is himself, those born of him, and the proofs of the Creator that he has witnessed and observed, and his transfer from one state to another and from one condition to another from the time of his birth until the time of his death. Then he specified the East and the West, because the rising of the sun from one of the two horizons and its setting in the other, on a straight measure through the seasons of the year and a level reckoning, is among the most evident things by which one can argue. And because of its clarity, the Friend of God (Khalil Allah, i.e. Abraham) moved to argue by it, rather than by giving life and causing death, against Nimrod ibn Kan'an, so the one who disbelieved was confounded. It has been read: "Lord of the Easts and the Wests." [Also read:] "Who was sent to you," with the hamza of alladhi... [the reading is with a fatha on the hamza].

Fa-in qulta: How did he say first "if you are certain" (in kuntum muqinin) and last "if you are reasoning" (in kuntum ta'qilun)? Qultu: He was gentle at first, but when he saw from them great stubbornness in obstinacy and little attentiveness to the presentation of proofs, he became harsh and retorted: "Your messenger is surely mad," with his saying: "if you are reasoning."

If you say: would "la-asjununnaka" (I will surely imprison you) not be shorter than "la-aj'alannaka mina l-masjunin" (I will surely make you among the imprisoned), and convey its meaning?

I answer: as for being shorter, yes. But as for conveying its meaning, no. For its meaning is: "I will make you one of those whose condition you know in my prisons." It was his custom to take whoever he wanted to imprison and cast him into a deep pit, extending far down into the earth, alone, where he could neither see nor hear. So that was more severe than killing, and more severe still.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verse 30–31:

The wāw in His saying, ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾ (awa-law ji'tuka) is the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), and the interrogative hamza has entered upon it. Its meaning is: "Would you do this to me even if I brought you something clear?" That is, "coming with a miracle" (jā'iyan bil-mu'jiza).

In His saying, ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ (in kunta mina al-ṣādiqīn), there is an indication that one who brings a miracle is none other than one truthful in his claim, because the miracle is a confirmation from God of the one claiming prophethood, and the Wise does not confirm a liar. It is strange that someone like Pharaoh would not have been unaware of this, yet it was hidden from some people of the qibla [[His saying "and it was hidden from some people of the qibla" means the People of the Sunnah, who said that both the good and the bad are by God's decree and predestination, and no absurdity followed for them, as explained in the science of tawhid. (ʿA.)]] who permitted that God do what is ugly, to the extent that they were compelled to accept the confirmation of liars through miracles.

Its estimated sense is: "If you are of the truthful in your claim, bring it," so the response (jawāb) is omitted, because the command to bring it indicates it.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 32–33:**

*A manifest serpent (thu'ban mubin)*: clearly a serpent, with nothing resembling a serpent about it, just as things falsified through sorcery and enchantment are. It is narrated that it turned into a snake that rose into the sky to the distance of a mile, then descended toward Pharaoh, advancing, and began to say: "O Moses, command me with whatever you wish." Pharaoh said: "I ask you by the one who sent you to take it." So he took it, and it returned to being a staff.

*"To the onlookers"*: this is evidence that its whiteness was something that drew the gaze of the spectators, because it was outside the ordinary course of things, and it was a luminous whiteness.

It is narrated that when Pharaoh saw the first sign, he said: "Is there any other?" Moses then brought out his hand and Pharaoh said to him: "What is this?" He said: "Your hand, so what is in it?" Then he put it under his armpit and drew it out, and it had a radiance that nearly overwhelms the sight[[The author's phrase "wa-lahā shuʿāʿ yakādu yaghshā al-abṣār" (it had a radiance that nearly overwhelms the sight): in al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari), "al-ghishāʾ" means a covering, end quote. The author's wording may be yaʿshā with the unpointed letter ʿayn, and in al-Sihah "al-ʿashā" (short vowel form) is a verbal noun of al-aʿshā, the one who cannot see at night but sees by day. (ʿ)]] and fills the horizon.

Q: What is the governing element (al-‘amil) of ḥawlahu?
A: It is in the accusative in two ways: a verbal accusative (naṣb fi al-lafẓ) and an accusative of position (naṣb fi al-maḥall), which is the accusative of circumstance (al-ḥāl). The governing element of the verbal accusative is what is implied within the adverb of place (al-ẓarf). The governing element of the accusative of position, namely the accusative of circumstance, is...

Let me correct my approach: the instruction is to translate the passage faithfully, so here is the translation.

**Translation:**

Q: What is the governing element (al-ʿāmil) of ḥawlahu?
A: It is in the accusative in two respects: an accusative in its wording (naṣb lafẓī) and an accusative in its position (naṣb maḥallī). The governing element of the verbal accusative is what is implied within the adverbial complement (al-ẓarf). The governing element of the accusative of position, which is the accusative of circumstance (al-ḥāl), is: He said, "Pharaoh was bewildered when he saw the two signs, and remained not knowing which of his two ends was longer, until the mention of his claim to divinity slipped from him, the pride of lordship fell from his shoulders, his muscles trembled, and his lungs swelled with fear and terror (In al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "al-siḥr" means the lung, and it is said of a coward: his lung has swollen.) And his submission to his people, whom by his claim were his slaves while he was their god, reached such a point that he began to consult them and to admit to them what he had feared and anticipated and sensed from the direction of Moses, peace be upon him, and his domination over his kingdom and land. His saying, ﴿Indeed this is a knowledgeable sorcerer﴾, is a statement that is baffling if it prevails and far-fetched if it is held to. ﴿Are you urging﴾ comes from consultation (al-mu'āmara), which is conferring, or from command (al-amr), which is the opposite of prohibition: they made the slaves into commanders and their Lord into one commanded, because of the extreme confusion and bewilderment that had taken hold of him. And "what" (mādhā) is in the accusative either because it has the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), or because it is an object of the verb in his saying: ﴿I commanded you the good﴾."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 36–37:

It is read as "arji'hu" and "arjihu" (with hamza and without hamza), and both are dialectal forms. It is said: "arja'tuhu" and "arjaytuhu," meaning "I delayed him," when I postponed him. From this comes "al-Murji'ah" (the Murji'ah, the sect that defers judgment). [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is to postpone it. From it comes al-Murji'ah, who do not pronounce definitively on the threat of punishment for the sinners, and say: 'They are deferred to God's command.'" Ahmad said: The paths of interpretation of irjā' became narrow for him, so that he cited the Murji'ah as evidence for it, and he turned this title over to the People of the Sunnah, for they are the ones who do not pronounce definitively on the threat of punishment for the sinful believers, and say: "Their affair is with God; if He wills, He will punish them, and if He wills, He will forgive them." If the Murji'ah are those who are believers by His words, exalted is He, "Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" — O God, then bear witness that we are Murji'ah.]] They are those who do not pronounce definitively on the threat of punishment for the sinners, and say: "They are deferred to God's command." The meaning is: postpone him, and [postpone] his confrontation until the time of the gathering of the magicians. It is also said: "Detain him," [and] "hashirin" (summoners) means guards who gather the magicians. [[His words "shurtan yahshuruna al-saharah" (guards who gather the magicians): al-shurt, with a vowel, means the guards; they were so named because they made for themselves a sign by which they would be recognized, as the Sihah (Lexicon) states. (Ayn)]] They answered his statement, "Indeed, this is a magician," with their words, "every skilled magician," using the word denoting totality and the form of intensification, so as to calm his mind and quiet some of his anxiety. al-A'mash read: "bi-kulli sahir" (every magician).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 38–40:

"The appointed day" (al-yawm al-ma'lum): the day of the festival (yawm al-zinah). Its appointed time (mi'qat): the time of mid-morning (waqt al-duha), because it is the time that Moses, upon him be blessings and peace, set for them on the day of the festival, in his saying: ﴿Your appointment is the day of the festival, and let the people be gathered at mid-morning﴾.

Al-mi'qat (the appointed time) is that for which a time or place is fixed, i.e. defined as a period of time or a place. From it comes the term mawaqit al-ihram (the fixed places for entering the state of ihram).

﴿Will you gather?﴾ is a urging on them to hasten in assembling, and the intended meaning is to hurry them and spur them on, just as a man says to his servant: "Are you going?" when he wants to stir him and urge him to set off, as though he imagines that the people have already set off while he is standing still. From this is the saying of Ta'abbata Sharran:

"Will you send Dinar for our need, or the slave of Rabb, a brother of Awn ibn Mikhraq?" [This is attributed to Ta'abbata Sharran, and it is also said to be by Jarir al-Khatafi. Hal (will you) is an interrogative of urging, containing an incitement to action. Dinar is the name of a man, and so is Abd Rabb; it is in the accusative as a conjunction with the position of Dinar, since it is an object in meaning. Akha Awf is its adjective. It is also said to be a vocative. Awf and Mikhraq are the names of two men. It is also narrated as "Awn" with a nun.]

He means: send him to us quickly and do not delay him. ﴿Perhaps we shall follow the sorcerers﴾, i.e. in their religion, if they overcome Moses, and we will not follow Moses in his religion. Their purpose is not to follow the sorcerers [the phrase "bi-ittiba' al-saharah" (in following the sorcerers) perhaps should read "ittiba'" (following), as in the expression of al-Nasafi. (Editor's note)], rather the general aim is that they should not follow Moses; so the speech is framed as a metonymy (kinayah), because if they follow the sorcerers they would not be following Moses, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 38–40:

"The appointed day" (al-yawm al-ma'lum): the day of the festival (yawm al-zinah). Its appointed time (mi'qat): the time of mid-morning (waqt al-duha), because it is the time that Moses, upon him be blessings and peace, set for them on the day of the festival, in his saying: ﴿Your appointment is the day of the festival, and let the people be gathered at mid-morning﴾.

Al-mi'qat (the appointed time) is that for which a time or place is fixed, i.e. defined as a period of time or a place. From it comes the term mawaqit al-ihram (the fixed places for entering the state of ihram).

﴿Will you gather?﴾ is a urging on them to hasten in assembling, and the intended meaning is to hurry them and spur them on, just as a man says to his servant: "Are you going?" when he wants to stir him and urge him to set off, as though he imagines that the people have already set off while he is standing still. From this is the saying of Ta'abbata Sharran:

Also read: naʿam, with the vowel of the ʿayn in kasra (i.e., naʿim) [[His words "and it was read naʿam with kasra" mean the ʿayn is vowelled with kasra, as in al-Sihah. (ʿA.)]]; the two are dialectal variants. Since His words "Surely for us there will indeed be a reward" carry the sense of the response to a conditional clause, by virtue of indicating it, and since His words "and surely you will indeed be among those brought near" are conjoined to it and fall under its ruling, the particle idhan (then) is placed in its proper position, that which the answer and recompense require. He promised them that to their reward for their sorcery, through which they reckoned they would prevail over Moses, would be added nearness to Him and closeness (al-qurba ʿindahu wa-l-zulfa).

They swore by the might of Pharaoh, and this is among the oaths of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam). Likewise, every oath sworn by other than God. In Islam, an oath is valid only when it is made by God, qualified by some of His names or attributes, such as your saying: "By God," "By the Most Merciful," "By my Lord," "By the Lord of the Throne," "By the might of God," "By the power of God," "By the majesty of God," "By the greatness of God." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not swear by your fathers, nor by your mothers, nor by the tawaghit (false objects of worship). Do not swear except by God, and do not swear by God except when you are truthful." [Narrated by al-Nasa'i from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, without his words "and do not swear except by God," and he said "by the andad (rivals)" instead of "tawaghit." He also has it from the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah: "Do not swear by your fathers, nor by the tawaghit," in abridged form. In the Two Sahihs, from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever is going to swear, let him swear only by God."]

People have, in this matter, innovated in their Islam an ignorance that has made the first ignorance forgotten. For if one of them swore by all of God's names and attributes concerning something, it would not be accepted from him, nor would it be counted, until he swore by the head of his ruler. If he swears by him, that is for them the "utmost oath" (jahd al-yamin), beyond which there is no oath for one who swears.

﴿What they fabricate﴾: that which they turn away from its face and its reality by their sorcery and their guile, and they falsify it, so that they make it appear, in their ropes and their staffs, as if they were serpents moving swiftly, through deception upon the onlookers. Or their "ifk" (fabrication): he called those things "ifk" as hyperbole (mubalaghah).

It is narrated that they said: "If what Musa has brought is sorcery, it will not prevail. And if it is from Allah, it will not remain hidden from us." Then, when he cast his staff, it swallowed up what they had brought, and they knew that it was from Allah, so they believed.

It is related from ʿIkrimah, may Allah be pleased with him: "They became sorcerers in the morning, and witnesses by evening."

He expressed their prostration by "casting" (ilqa’) only because it was mentioned together with the other "castings," so he took the path of mushakalah (congruity of expression, i.e., using a word in harmony with a preceding one). Also, while observing mushakalah, it is implied that when they saw what they saw, they could not restrain themselves from throwing themselves down to the ground in prostration, as if they had been seized and thrown down.

If you ask: who is the agent of the casting, if it were stated explicitly? I say: it is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through the success He granted them. Or [it is] their faith. Or [it is] the dazzling miracles they witnessed. You may also not posit any agent, since ﴿alqū﴾ (أَلْقُوا) means "they fell prostrate and dropped down" (kharrū wa saqaṭū).

﴿Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) for ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, because Pharaoh, may the curse of Allah be upon him, claimed lordship (rububiyyah), so they wished to dismiss him from that claim. The meaning of its attribution to the two of them in that context is: He is the One to whom these two call, and the One through whose hands He carried out what He carried out.

Then you will soon know, i.e., the consequence (wabal) of what you did.

The harm (ḍurr), the ḍayr and the ḍawr are one and the same. They meant: "There is no harm to us in that; rather, there is for us in it the greatest benefit, from what is achieved for us through patience in it for the sake of Allah: the expiation of sins, a great reward, and many compensations."

Or: "There is no harm to us in what you threaten us with, namely killing, for we must return to our Lord by some cause of death, and killing is the easiest of its causes and the most hopeful." Or: "There is no harm to us in your killing us; if you kill us, we shall return to our Lord in the manner of one who hopes for His forgiveness and longs for His mercy, because of what He has granted us of precedence in faith." The predicate (khabar) is omitted. The meaning is: "There is no harm in that," or "upon us," (ʿalaynā) in the sense of "because we were..." (an kunnā), that is, "because we were the first group of believers in their time, or among Pharaoh's subjects, or among the people of the assembly."

It is also read as in kunnā, with a kasra, which is the conditional (sharṭ) used by one who is confident in his matter and certain of its soundness. They were certain that they were the first of the believers. A parallel is the words of a worker to one who delays his wage: "If I have worked for you, then pay me my due." Similarly is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿If you have gone forth in jihad in My cause and seeking My pleasure﴾, although He knows that they went forth only for that.

Read in two ways: "Asra" with the hamza cut, and "Sara" with it joined. ﴿Indeed you will be pursued﴾ gives the reason for the command to travel by night: Pharaoh and his soldiers will follow their tracks. The meaning is that I designed the plan for your affair and theirs so that you would go ahead and they would follow you, until they entered where you had entered and took the same route through the sea. Then I closed the sea over them and destroyed them.

It is related that on that night every house of theirs had a child who died, so they were occupied with their dead until Musa left with his people.

It is also related that God revealed to Musa: "Gather the Children of Israel, four households to a house. Then slaughter a young goat (al-jada') and strike its blood on your doors, for I will command the angels not to enter any house with blood on its door, and I will command them to kill the firstborn of the Copts. Bake unleavened bread (khubzan fatiran), for it is quicker for you. Then travel by night with My servants until you reach the sea, and My command will come to you."

Pharaoh sent after them a million and five hundred thousand crowned kings (malik musawwar), with each king having a thousand men. Pharaoh himself set out in a great host, and his vanguard was seven hundred thousand, each man on a horse with a helmet on his head. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that Pharaoh set out with a million horses apart from the mares. This is why the people of Musa, who were six hundred and seventy thousand, seemed few to him, and he called them ﴿a small band﴾.

﴿Indeed these﴾ is quoted in direct speech after an implied verb of saying. A shirdhima (small band) is a small group. From it comes their saying: "a garment shara-dhim," meaning one that is torn and cut into pieces.

He described them as few in several ways. He expressed them by the word shirdhima, which indicates fewness. Then he described them with the attribute of being few. Then he put that attribute in the plural so that each part of them would be shown to be few. And he chose the sound plural form, which is used for paucity (jam' al-salama, the sound plural, which is for small numbers). The word qalil (few) may also take the plural forms aqilla and qilal, as in sarir (bed) with its plurals surur and so on.

It is also permissible that by qilla he means abasement and lowliness, not a small number. The meaning would then be that because of their weakness no attention is paid to them, and their defeat or ascendancy is not expected. But they do acts that anger us and constrict our breasts. We are a people whose habit is vigilance, caution, and the exercise of firm judgment in affairs. So when someone rebels against us, we hasten to end his corruption. These are excuses he offered to the people of the cities, lest they think that his power and authority had been weakened.

It is also read as ﴿hadhirun﴾, ﴿ha'dhirun﴾ and ﴿hadirun﴾ (with a dal not dotted). In al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari) it is said: "It is read: ﴿wa-inna lajami'un hadhirun﴾ (And indeed we are a wary host), and hadhirun, also with a dammed dhal, transmitted by al-Akhfash. The meaning of ha'dhirun is 'ready prepared.' And in it: 'a man adda,' meaning he became strong, from al-adah (instrument), so he is mu'addin with a hamza, that is, one who bears arms. And it contains: 'I adaytu the journey, so I am mu'addin to it,' when I have prepared myself for it." (ʿ)

So hadhir means alert, and ha'dhir means one who renews his caution. It is also said that the mu'addi is one armed with weapons, and he does this out of caution and to protect himself. Hadir means stout and strong. A poet said:

"I love the bad boy for his mother's sake,
and I hate him when she hates him, though he is hadir."

The hadir is strong and powerful, or brave and bold. That is, the love of the child depends on the love of his mother, not on his good qualities. The pronoun in "abghadahu" (and I hate him) refers to the boy without his attributes. But this is the disposition of one who is wholly absorbed in love of women.

The meaning is that they are strong and mighty. It is also said that they are fully armed, and that their weapons have made their bodies firm and hardened.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 57–60:

On the authority of Mujahid: he called them "treasures" because they had not spent from them in obedience to God. "Maqam" means place; he intends: the good dwellings and the splendid gatherings. On the authority of al-Dahhak: the pulpits. It has been said that "al-sirr" in ﴿the chambers﴾ [[His saying "and it has been said: al-sirr in al-hijal": al-sirr means intercourse, and al-hijal is the plural of hijla, which is the bride's chamber decorated with garments, couches and curtains, as stated in al-Sihah. (Editor's note)]] ﴿Thus it was﴾ may carry three aspects. The accusative: "We caused them to leave in the same manner as that departure which We have described." The genitive, as an attribute of "maqam": "a noble station like that station which they had." The nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject: "the matter is so." ﴿So they pursued them﴾: they caught up with them. It is also read: ﴿fa-atba'uhum﴾ [and they pursued them], ﴿at sunrise﴾: entering the time of sunrise, from "the sun rose" (sharaqat al-shams, shurukan) when it appeared.

﴿He will guide me.﴾ That is, to the way of deliverance from their pursuit and harm. It is also read: ﴿فَلَمَّا تَرَاءَى الْجَمْعَانِ﴾ (*fa-lamma tarāʾā al-jamʿān*, "When the two hosts saw each other"). ﴿إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ﴾ (*innā la-mudrakūn*, "We will surely be overtaken") is read with the *dal* doubled and the *ra* vowelled with a kasra, from *iddaraka al-shayʾ*, meaning a thing followed in succession until it perishes. From the same root is His saying: ﴿بَلِ ادَّارَكَ عِلْمُهُمْ فِي الْآخِرَةِ﴾ ("Rather, their knowledge of the Hereafter has been exhausted," Q. 27:66). Al-Hasan said: "They were ignorant of the knowledge of the Hereafter." In the same sense is the verse from the *Hamasa* (the anthology of Abu Tammam):

*After the sons of my mother, those who followed one another,*
*Do I hope for life, or do I dread death?*

*They were eight, the crest of their people;*
*Through them I would give what I wished, and withhold.*

*Those were my brothers of pure friendship; I was bereaved of them,*
*And the palm is nothing but finger upon finger.*

These lines are by Abu al-Hanak al-Bara', Rabʿi al-Fiqʿsi. The *hamza* is an interrogative of disapproval, and the intended meaning is grief and sorrow. *Tatābaʿū* means they died out one after another. *Arḥā* means: "Do I hope for a life, or do I dread death?", i.e., I will not do that after them. He said "my mother's sons" because the context is one of tenderness and compassion. They were eight, the leaders of their people, like the *dhuʾāba* (the forelock), which is the hair of the head that moves about it; this is an eloquent metaphor. Then he said: "Through them I would do what I wished, giving and withholding." It is also permissible to make both verbs passive, so the meaning becomes: "Through them I would attain what I wished, and be protected from the harm of what I wished." *Razaʾtuhu* means I was struck in his property. *Razaʾtuhu māluhu*: his property was taken from him. *Razaʾtuhum* is passive, meaning: time diminished them for me and took them from me, so I have no strength after them, just as when the palm loses its fingers its strength is gone, for its grip is only through fingers arranged in order. They are to me as fingers are to the palm.

The meaning is: "We will indeed be successively destroyed at their hands, until none of us remains." *Al-Fariq* is the separated part of it. It is also read: *kullu falaq*, and the meaning is the same. *Al-Ṭawd* is the great mountain [[His words "al-Ṭawd: the great mountain rising high in the sky." In the *Sihah* (of al-Jawhari): "ṭawd among the mountains," like ṭawf and ṭawḥ. *Al-maṭāwid* is the pattern of *al-maṭāwiḥ*. (ʿ)]] rising in the sky. ﴿وَأَزْلَفْنَا ثَمَّ الْآخَرِينَ﴾ ("And We brought near there the others"), in the place where the sea split: ﴿الْآخَرِينَ﴾ refers to the people of Pharaoh, meaning We brought them near to the Children of Israel; or, We drew some of them close to others and gathered them so that none of them would escape; or, We advanced them to the sea. It is also read *wa-azlaqnā* with a *qaf*, meaning We made their feet slip. The meaning is: We removed their might. Compare the verse:

*You two reconciled ʿAbs when its throne had been demolished,*
*And Dhubyān when its sandals slipped from their feet.*

[[This is by Zuhayr, praising Harim ibn Sinan and al-Harith ibn ʿAwf. ʿAbs and Dhubyān are both names of tribes. He says: you two reconciled these two tribes by making peace between them and paying the blood-money for their slain. "Had demolished its throne": that is, had pulled down its throne. This is an image for the loss of their might and the end of their rule.

"The sandal slipped from the foot": it slid from its place. This is also an image for the disruption of their affairs and the corruption of their judgment. In the verse there is a kind of *ṭibāq* (antithesis), since the first [tribe] was struck by punishment from above its heads, and the second by punishment from beneath its feet.]] It is also possible that God makes their path in the sea other than what He made for the Children of Israel, a dry way, so that He causes them to slip in it.

It is reported from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib that Jibril, peace be upon him, was between the Children of Israel and the family of Pharaoh. He would say to the Children of Israel: "Let your last join your first." And he would face the Copts and say: "Slowly, let your last join your first." When Musa reached the sea, a believer from the family of Pharaoh, who was before Musa, said to him: "Where were you commanded? This sea is before you and the family of Pharaoh has overtaken you." He said: "I was commanded to go by the sea," and Musa did not know what to do. So God, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Strike the sea with your staff." He struck it, and it became twelve paths in it, one path for each tribe.

It is also related that Yusha' said: "O Speaker of God, where were you commanded? Pharaoh has overtaken us and the sea is before us." Musa said: "Here." So Yusha' entered the water, and Musa struck the sea with his staff, and they entered. It is related that Musa said at that moment: "O You who were before everything, who brought everything into being, and who exists after everything." It is said that this sea is the Sea of Qulzum. It is also said that it is a sea beyond Egypt called Asaf.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 26, verses 72–73:

It is necessary in ﴿هل يسمعونكم﴾ to posit an elided genitive-modifier (muḍāf), meaning: "Do they hear your supplication?" Qatada read ﴿يسمعونكم﴾ (yasma'ūnakum), meaning: "Do they hear you, i.e., do they give you an answer to your supplication? And are they able to do that?" It came in the present tense (muḍāri') while being placed within ﴿إذ﴾ (idh) to depict a past state as if it were present (ḥikāyat al-ḥāl al-māḍiya). Its meaning: call to mind the past circumstances in which you used to call upon them, and say: "Did they ever hear, or make [anyone] hear, at all?" And this is more effective in rebuke (tabkīt).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 74–82:

When they answered him with the answer of those who follow their fathers blindly, he said to them: Carry this matter of your blind following to its furthest end, which is the worship of your earliest ancestors, the first ones of your fathers. For precedence and antiquity are not proof of correctness, and falsehood does not become truth through age. The worship of anyone who worships these idols is nothing but the worship of enemies to Him. The meaning of enmity is found in the words of the Exalted: ﴿No indeed! They will deny their worship of them and become opponents to them﴾ [19:82]. Also, the one who incites to worship them is the greatest enemy of man, namely Satan. He said "an enemy to me" only to depict the matter as it stood within himself, meaning: I reflected on my affair and saw that my worship of them was worship of an enemy, so I avoided it and preferred the worship of the One from whom all good comes. By this he showed them that it was counsel with which he first counselled himself, and upon which he built the management of his own affair, so that they would consider and say: Abraham gave us counsel only with what he gave counsel to himself, and he wanted for us only what he wanted for his own soul. This makes it more likely that they would accept it and more inclined to listen to him. Had he said "for indeed he is an enemy to you," it would not have had this effect. Moreover, he entered it through the door of allusion (ta'ridh), and allusion to the one being advised can reach what explicit statement does not reach, because he reflects upon it, and reflection may lead him to acceptance. From this is what is related about al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, that a man confronted him with something, and he said: "If you were in the place you are in, you would need to be disciplined." And a man heard people talking about al-Hijr and said: "It is neither my house nor your house." The words "enemy" (ʿaduww) and "friend" (ṣadīq) may be used with the meaning of singular and plural. He said:

And a people with power over me, whom I see as enemies though they were friends.

[The "mirra" means strength and intensity of dispute; it is also narrated as "mabarra," meaning enmity, boasting or intensity. "ʿAduww" and "ṣadīq" are used for the masculine, feminine, dual and plural. He says: many a people who hold power over me, I see them today as enemies, though they were friends.]

From this is His saying: ﴿And they are an enemy to you﴾ [26:77], where the word is used in the manner of verbal nouns (maṣādir) for parallelism, like "al-qabūl" (acceptance) and "al-walūʿ" (fondness), and "al-ḥanīn" (yearning) and "al-ṣahīl" (neighing). ﴿Except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [26:77] is a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ, an exception not belonging to the same category as what precedes it), as if he said: "But the Lord of the worlds." ﴿Then it is He who guides me﴾ [26:78] means: when He completed his creation and breathed the spirit into him, He followed that with His continuous guidance, which never ceases, toward everything that makes him fit and concerns him. Otherwise, who guided him to be nourished by blood in the womb by suction? Who guided him to recognise the breast at birth, to know its place, and to know the manner of suckling, and other guidances of livelihood and of the hereafter? He said ﴿and when I am ill﴾ [26:80] rather than "when He makes me ill" because many causes of illness arise from a person's failure in what he eats and drinks. Then the sages said: If most of the dead were asked, "What is the cause of your deaths?" they would say: "Overeating (al-takhamm)."

It is read "khaṭāyāy" (my faults), and what is meant is what occasionally slips from them of minor sins, because the prophets are protected from major sins and chosen above the worlds. It has been said that these are His words: ﴿I am sick﴾ [37:89], and His words ﴿Rather, it was done by their biggest one﴾ [21:63], and His words to Sarah: "She is my sister." These are only allusive speeches (maʿārīḍ al-kalām) and fabrications for the disbelievers, and they are not faults that call for seeking forgiveness.

If you say: If the prophets commit only minor sins, and these are expiated, why did he affirm for himself a fault or faults, and hope that they would be forgiven? I say: The answer is what I mentioned earlier: the seeking of forgiveness by the prophets is humility before their Lord and self-abasement, and this is shown by His words ﴿I hope﴾ [26:82], and he did not state definitively the forgiveness. In this there is also instruction for their communities, so that they may be gentle with them in avoiding disobedience and in guarding against it, and in seeking forgiveness for what slips from them.

If you say: Why did He tie the forgiveness of faults to the Day of Judgement, when they are forgiven in this world? I say: Because their effect becomes clear on that day, while now it is hidden and not known.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 74–82:

When they answered him with the answer of those who follow their fathers blindly, he said to them: Carry this matter of your blind following to its furthest end, which is the worship of your earliest ancestors, the first ones of your fathers. For precedence and antiquity are not proof of correctness, and falsehood does not become truth through age. The worship of anyone who worships these idols is nothing but the worship of enemies to Him. The meaning of enmity is found in the words of the Exalted: ﴿No indeed! They will deny their worship of them and become opponents to them﴾ [19:82]. Also, the one who incites to worship them is the greatest enemy of man, namely Satan. He said "an enemy to me" only to depict the matter as it stood within himself, meaning: I reflected on my affair and saw that my worship of them was worship of an enemy, so I avoided it and preferred the worship of the One from whom all good comes. By this he showed them that it was counsel with which he first counselled himself, and upon which he built the management of his own affair, so that they would consider and say: Abraham gave us counsel only with what he gave counsel to himself, and he wanted for us only what he wanted for his own soul. This makes it more likely that they would accept it and more inclined to listen to him. Had he said "for indeed he is an enemy to you," it would not have had this effect. Moreover, he entered it through the door of allusion (ta'ridh), and allusion to the one being advised can reach what explicit statement does not reach, because he reflects upon it, and reflection may lead him to acceptance. From this is what is related about al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, that a man confronted him with something, and he said: "If you were in the place you are in, you would need to be disciplined." And a man heard people talking about al-Hijr and said: "It is neither my house nor your house." The words "enemy" (ʿaduww) and "friend" (ṣadīq) may be used with the meaning of singular and plural. He said:

And a people with power over me, whom I see as enemies though they were friends.

[The "mirra" means strength and intensity of dispute; it is also narrated as "mabarra," meaning enmity, boasting or intensity. "ʿAduww" and "ṣadīq" are used for the masculine, feminine, dual and plural. He says: many a people who hold power over me, I see them today as enemies, though they were friends.]

Otherwise, who guided him to be nourished by blood in the womb by suction? Who guided him to recognise the breast at birth, to know its place, and to know the manner of suckling, and other guidances of livelihood and of the hereafter?
