Al-Hukm: the wisdom, or judgment between people in truth. It was also said to mean prophethood, because the prophet possesses wisdom and judges between the servants of God. Joining him to the righteous (al-ilhaq bi'l-salihin) means that God grants him success in a deed by which he is counted among them, or brings him together with them in Paradise. God answered his prayer when he said ﴿And indeed, he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ Al-ikhza' comes from al-khizy, which is humiliation. It may also come from al-khizaya [[The editor's note on "ومن الخزاية" reads: perhaps "or from". (ʿA.)]], which is shame. This is also like their seeking forgiveness for what they know is already forgiven. The pronoun in ﴿the day they are resurrected﴾ refers to the servants, since it is known. Or it refers to the misguided. It may also be taken as part of the plea for forgiveness for his father, meaning: "Do not disgrace me on the day the misguided are resurrected, and my father among them." [[The editor's note reads: this is probably a grammatical reading of the sense, as if he said: "It is possible that the pronoun refers to the misguided... etc." (ʿA.)]]

﴿Except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ — "illa" here is a substitution-like exception with "man" as its referent, and "hal" (circumstantial state) is the sense: the one who comes to God in a state of a sound heart. This is like the line of poetry:

"Their greeting among them is painful striking,
and its reward is nothing but the sword."

Its explanation is that someone asks you, "Does Zayd have wealth and sons?" and you reply, "His wealth and his sons: the soundness of his heart," meaning you negate wealth and sons from him and affirm soundness of heart for him in their place. If you wish, you may take the sentence according to its meaning and understand wealth and sons as meaning riches, as if it were said: "On a day when riches will not benefit, except the riches of one who comes to God with a sound heart," because a man's richness in his religion is through the soundness of his heart, just as his richness in his worldly life is through his wealth and sons.

You may also make the exception disconnected (munqati', i.e., not of the same kind as what precedes it). In that case you must also supply an implied annexed noun (al-mudaf), which is "the state," and what is meant is the soundness of the heart. It is not of the same kind as wealth and sons, so the meaning does not turn into "wealth and sons do not benefit, but the soundness of the heart does." If the annexed noun is not supplied, the exception has no meaning. It is also said that "man" is the object of "yanfa'" (benefits), meaning: no wealth and no sons benefit, except a man whose heart is sound along with his wealth, in that he spent it in obedience to God, and along with his sons, in that he guided them to religion and taught them the laws. On this reading, it is also permissible to read ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ as meaning sound from the trial of wealth and sons. The meaning of the soundness of the heart is its being free from the ailments of disbelief and sins. God honored His friend (Khalil) with this and indicated the high rank of his sincerity: He related his exception in the form of one who is pleased with his success in it, and then made it an attribute of him in His saying ﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham, when he came to his Lord with a sound heart.﴾

Among the strange interpretations is that of some who explained "salim" (sound) as "one stung by fear of God." Another opinion holds that it means one who was safe (salima), who gave safety (sallama), who submitted (aslama), who was at peace (salim), and who surrendered (istaslama).

How excellent is the order Abraham, peace be upon him, gave to his speech with the polytheists. First he asked them what they worship, as a question establishing a point rather than seeking information. Then he turned against their gods and nullified their status by showing that they neither harm nor benefit, neither see nor hear, and that they merely follow their forefathers in imitation. Thus he broke their claim and removed it from being even a doubt, let alone a proof. Then he depicted the matter within himself, apart from them, until he came out of it to the mention of God, the Mighty and Exalted. He magnified God's majesty and enumerated His blessings, from the time of His creating and originating him until his death, together with what is hoped for in the Hereafter of His mercy. Then he followed that with supplications of the sincere, and humbly implored Him with the humility of the penitent. Then he connected it with the mention of the Day of Resurrection, God's reward and punishment, and what the polytheists will be brought to on that day of regret and sorrow over the error they were in, and of wishing to return to the world so that they might believe and obey.

"Their greeting among them is painful striking,
and its reward is nothing but the sword."

Its explanation is that someone asks you, "Does Zayd have wealth and sons?" and you reply, "His wealth and his sons: the soundness of his heart," meaning you negate wealth and sons from him and affirm soundness of heart for him in their place. Then he connected it with the mention of the Day of Resurrection, God's reward and punishment, and what the polytheists will be brought to on that day of regret and sorrow over the error they were in, and of wishing to return to the world so that they might believe and obey.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 90–95:

The Garden is brought near to the station of the blessed, who look at it and rejoice that they are those who are gathered toward it; and the Fire is made manifest and exposed to the wretched, in plain sight of them, and they lament that they are those who are driven toward it. God Most High said: ﴿And the Garden is brought near for the God-fearing, not far away﴾, and He said: ﴿But when they see it brought near, the faces of those who disbelieved will be darkened﴾.

All the distresses and regrets gather upon them, for the Fire is placed in plain sight of them, so they perish of grief at every moment. They are rebuked for their polytheism, and it is said to them: ﴿Where are your gods? Can they help you, or help themselves?﴾ That is, by their support of you, or by their own victory, since they and their gods are the fuel of the Fire. This is His saying: ﴿So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators﴾. That is, the gods, and ﴿those who went astray﴾, meaning their worshippers, ﴿and the hosts of Iblis all together﴾, to whom Hell is made manifest.

Al-Kabkabah (the repeated tumbling) is the repetition of kabb (to overturn). Repetition in the wording is taken as evidence of repetition in meaning, as if, when they are cast into Hell, they are overturned again and again until they settle at its bottom. O God, protect us from it, O best of those from whom protection is sought.

﴿And the hosts of Iblis, all of them﴾: his devils, or those who follow him from the rebellious among the jinn and humankind.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 105–110:

The word "qawm" (people) is feminine, and its diminutive is "quwaymah." The parallel to His saying "al-mursalin" (the messengers), where what is meant is Nuh (peace be upon him), is your saying:

"So-and-so rides the beasts and wears the striped cloaks, yet he has nothing but one beast and one cloak."

[[Mahmud said: "What is meant is Nuh, just as you say: 'So-and-so rides the beasts and wears the striped cloaks, yet he has nothing but one beast and one cloak.'" Ahmad said: There is no need to interpret the plural as singular here, given the certainty that whoever denies one messenger has denied all the messengers, for there is no prophet except that the proof of his truthfulness rests on the miracle that indicates truth. So they have denied everyone whose truthfulness rests on the proof of miracle. Likewise the indication in His saying, "We make no distinction between any of His messengers" (2:285), because distinguishing between them requires denying all of them, and affirming one requires affirming all of them. And God knows best.]] It was said: "their brother" (akhahum), because he was one of them, from the speech of the Arabs: "O brother of the Banu Tamim," meaning "O one of them." And from this is the verse in the Hamasah:

"A people who, when evil bares its fangs at them, rush toward it in groups and singly,
They do not ask their brother, when he calls them in calamities, for proof of what he says."

It is by Liqrit ibn Unayf from the tribe of Ul-Anbar. Some men of the Banu Shayban raided him and took thirty camels from him. He sought help from his people, but they did not help him. So he appealed to the Banu Mazin, and they rode with him, drove off one hundred camels from the Banu Shayban, and escorted him back to his people. He then praised them and rebuked his own people.

Al-nājidh (the molar tooth) is the tooth between the molar and the canine; it is also said to be the wisdom tooth, and it is also said to be any molar. Al-zarafah, with fatha or damma, is a group of people, and from it the well-known animal was named. Al-wuḥdān, with damma, is the plural of wāḥid (one). He likened evil to a lion baring its canines, by way of metaphor (al-makniyyah), and then attributed to it the molars by way of imagination (takhyīl). He says: the Banu Mazin are brave: when evil appears and intensifies, they rush to it in groups and singly. He used "flying" for this by way of explicit metaphor (al-tasrīḥiyyah). Or he likened them to birds in speed and spreading, by way of implicit metaphor (kināyah), and the mode is imagination. They do not ask their companion for proof of what he says when he calls them, raising his voice, in times of calamity.

"Trustworthy among them" (amīn): he was known for trustworthiness among them, like Muhammad (ﷺ) among Quraysh.

"And obey me" (wa-aṭī'ūnī): in my counsel to you and in what I call you to of the truth.

"For it (ʿalayhi)": on this matter, and on what I am engaged in, meaning: my calling and my counsel.

The meaning of "So fear God and obey me": fear God in obeying me. He repeated it to emphasize it upon them and to fix it in their souls, while attaching to each of the two a reason: the reason for the first is that he is trustworthy among them, and for the second, cutting off any expectation of reward from them.

And it is read: **وأتباعك** (*wa-atbāʿuka*), the plural of *tābiʿ*, like *shāhid* and *ashhād*. Or it is the plural of *tabaʿ*, like *baṭal* and *abṭāl*. The *wāw* is the *wāw al-ḥāl* (the circumstantial *wāw*, introducing a clause describing the state of the subject). Its proper form is that *qad* is understood after it, as in **وَاتَّبَعَكَ** (*wa-ittabaʿaka*). The word **الأرذل** has been pluralized both in the sound plural and in the broken plural in His saying ﴿Shall we believe you, when the lowest ones follow you?﴾ and in ﴿those who are our lowly ones﴾. **الرذالة والنذالة**: baseness and meanness.

They looked down on them only because of the lowliness of their lineage and their small share of worldly goods. It is said that they were of the people of base crafts (*al-ṣināʿāt al-daniyya*) [[Al-Zamakhsharī's phrase "al-ṣināʿāt al-daniyya" is perhaps "al-daniyya" (the lowly), as in al-Nasafī's wording. (Editor)]], such as weaving and cupping. But a craft does not diminish one's religion. This is how Quraysh spoke of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The followers of the prophets have always been like this, until it became one of their marks and signs. Do you not see that when Heraclius asked Abū Sufyān about the followers of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he replied, "The weak among the people and their lowly ones," he said: "The followers of the prophets have always been like this"? [[Agreed upon (*muttafaq ʿalayh*), from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, from Abū Sufyān, with the wording: "I asked you whether the weak among the people follow him or their nobles? I said: Rather, their weak. Such are the followers of the messengers." I say: he narrated it with the wording "their lowly ones" (*arādhilahum*). (Editor's note: the text reads "arādhilahum" in this narration.)]]

And from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: they are the *ghāgha* [[The phrase "al-ghāgha" is perhaps "al-ṣāgha" (goldsmiths). In al-Khāzin: Ibn ʿAbbās said: meaning the *qāfa* (trackers). (Editor)]]. From ʿIkrima: the weavers and the cobblers. From Muqātil: the lowly commoners.

﴿And what is my knowledge, and what thing is my knowledge?﴾ The meaning is the negation of his knowledge of the sincerity of their deeds toward God, and of his being informed of the secret of their affair and its inner reality. He said this because they had criticized his faith, despite their own lowliness, and claimed that they had not believed through reflection and insight, but had believed through whim and first impression, as God related of them in His saying: ﴿Those who are our lowest, following their first opinion﴾. It is permissible that Noah, peace be upon him, feigned ignorance toward them, so that he interpreted their saying "the lowest" by what lowliness is in his own view, namely evil deeds and corrupt beliefs, and did not heed what lowliness is in their view. Then he built his answer on that, saying: my duty is only to consider the outward, without searching into their secrets or splitting open their hearts. If they have an evil deed, God will call them to account and recompense them for it, and I am only a warner, neither a reckoner nor a recompenser. ﴿If only you perceived﴾ that, but you are ignorant, so you are driven along by ignorance wherever it steers you. He intended by this to refute their belief and to deny that the believer should be called lowly, even if he is the poorest of people and lowest in lineage, for richness is the richness of religion, and lineage is the lineage of piety.

﴿And I am not one to drive away the believers﴾. He means: it is not for me to follow your desires and please your souls by driving away the believers whose faith is sound, out of hope for your faith. And my duty is only to warn you with a clear warning, by means of the sound proof by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. Then you yourselves know better about your own affair.

Not a report of their denial (since he knows that the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed is more knowing), but he meant: I do not call upon You against them because they enraged and harmed me; rather I call upon You for your sake and for the sake of your religion, and because they denied me in Your revelation and Your message. ﴿So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾. Al-Fattahah (the judgment, al-hukuma): and al-Fattah (the judge, al-hakim), because he opens what is closed, just as he is named Faysal (the decider), because he separates between disputes. Al-Fulk (the ship): and its plural is fulk. Allah Most High said: ﴿And you see the ships therein plowing through [the waves]﴾. So the singular is on the pattern of qufl, and the plural is on the pattern of asad: they broke fa'l into fu'l just as they broke fa'l into fu'l, because the two are siblings in your saying: al-'Arab and al-'Arab, and al-Rushd and al-Rushd. So they said: asad and asad, and fulk and fulk. Its parallel is: ba'ir hijan and ibl hijan, and dir' dalas and duru' dalas, where the singular is on the pattern of kinaz and the plural on the pattern of kiram. Al-Mashhun: the filled up. It is said: he filled them against them with horsemen and footmen.

*"In the mirage, which raises them and lowers them... a ray' gleams as if it were a sahl."* [[Al-Musayyib ibn 'Alas. *Al-Al* is the mirage. It is also said that *al-al* is what appears as a mirage at the beginning and middle of the day.

*Al-Ray'* with a kasra means the road and the elevated part of the land. *Al-Sahl* is a white type of Yemeni cloth. The pronoun may refer to the caravan women (*al-zaʿaʾin*), meaning: they are in the mirage, or at its time, raising them at one time and lowering them at another. *Ray'* means an elevated road at one time and a low one at another.

Or it means a high place which one rises by climbing and descends from by going down. *Yalūh* means it appears from afar, as if it were white garments.]]

From this comes their saying, "How high is your land (*kam ray' arḍuka*)?", meaning its elevation. *Al-āya* means the landmark. They were among those who guided themselves by the stars during their journeys, so they set up tall landmarks on their roads and played with them, because they were independent of them by the stars.

From Mujahid: "They built on every high place pigeon-towers (*burūj al-ḥamām*)." [[Mahmud said: "They used to be guided on their journeys by the stars, so they set up landmarks on their roads and were frivolous in doing so, since the stars sufficed them. It is also said that what is meant is lofty palaces, and it is said: pigeon-towers." Ahmad said: The interpretation as palaces is more evident, and the blaming of such building has been related in the words of our Prophet (ﷺ), where he described those who will live at the end of time as boasting in building. How fine is the saying of Malik (may Allah be pleased with him): "The imam should not lead prayer from a place higher than where his companions stand, like the raised platforms in the mihrab (*al-dakakk*), which are very high, because they are frivolous." He expressed their elevation over the worshippers in the mihrab as a display of arrogance and of overtopping the followers with frivolity, just as Hud (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) described the elevation of his people in building as frivolity. As for interpreting the verse as setting up landmarks on the roads, when they had sufficient guidance from the stars, this is far-fetched, since need calls for such landmarks during dense cloud and similar conditions.

Had this been placed in our time for this purpose, it would not have been frivolous, and Allah knows best.]] *Al-maṣāniʿ* are water-reservoirs. It is also said they are lofty palaces and fortresses. *La'allakum takhludūn* means: you hope to remain forever in this world, or your state resembles the state of one who will live forever. In the reading of Ubayy: *ka'annakum* (as if you). It is also read *takhludūn* with a short, unstressed *ta'*, and also with a doubled *ta'*. *Wa-idhā baṭashtum* means: striking with a whip or a sword, that would be oppression and haughtiness. It is also said: the tyrant who kills and strikes in anger. From al-Hasan: "You rush to hasten the punishment, not pausing to reflect on the consequences."

He pressed hard in admonishing them about God's blessings: he summarized them and then detailed them, citing their own knowledge. He roused them from the heedlessness they were sunk in about these blessings when he said ﴿Aided you with what you know﴾ [[His words "حين قال" are probably "حيث قال" (where he said). (ʿ)]]. Then he enumerated them for them and made the Benefactor known to them by counting the blessings of His that they know, and [he made known] that just as He is able to bestow this blessing upon you, so He is able to reward and punish, so fear Him.

Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And God warns you of Himself, and God is Kind to His servants﴾. If you say: How did He join the sons with the cattle? I say: They are the ones who help them in guarding them and tending to them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 136–140:

If you say: "If it had been said, 'Whether you admonish or do not admonish,' it would have been more concise, and the meaning would be the same." I reply: The meaning is not the same; there is a difference between them. The intended meaning is: "It is all the same to us whether you have done this act, which is admonition, or whether you were never among its people or practitioners at all." This is more emphatic in showing how little they value his admonition than your saying, "or do you not admonish?"

As for the one who reads خَلْقُ الْأَوَّلِينَ (khalq al-awwalin) with a fatha on the khaa' (khalqu/khalaqa being read as a single word with the vowel fatha, so the reading is *khalaq*), its meaning is: what you have brought is the fabrication and invention of the ancients, as they said, "myths of the ancients." Or: "This is nothing but the creation of the earlier generations; we live as they lived and die as they died, and there is no resurrection and no reckoning."

As for the one who reads خُلُقُ (khuluq) with two dammas, and the one who reads it with one damma (khuluq / khuluq), its meaning is: "This religion we are upon is nothing but the custom and practice of the ancients; they professed it and believed in it, and we follow them." Or: "This life and death which we are upon, and this return, is what people have remained upon since ancient times." Or: "What you have brought is nothing but falsehood, the habit of the ancients, who used to fabricate the like of it and write it down."

Will you be left secure in what you have here? (This may be a rebuke against their being left to remain forever in their bounty, not leaving it, and it may be a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free, along with the gardens and what else they enjoy, with safety and ease.) "Fi ma huna" ("in what is here") refers to the bounty settled in this place. Then He explained it with His words: "in gardens and springs," and this too is a general statement followed by detail.

If you ask: why did He say "and date palms" after "in gardens," when the word "gardens" first includes date palms, just as the word "camels" includes camels among other livestock? In the same way, they mention "the garden" and mean only the date palms, just as they mention "the bounty" and mean only the camels. Zuhayr said: "... watered by a garden of palms..." (The explanation of this verse was given in the first volume, page 105, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.)

I say: there are two views. First, that the date palms are singled out by mentioning them separately after being included among the rest of the trees, to point out that they are distinguished from the others by their excellence. Second, that by "gardens" he means other trees, since the word allows for this, and then "date palms" is joined to them.

"Tal'ah" (the spathe) is what emerges from the palm tree, like the blade of a sword in its sheath, with the clusters of the qinw (the bunch) inside it. The qinw is the name for what comes out of the trunk, together with its stalk and its strands. "Hadim" means delicate and slender, from the saying "kashh hadim" (a slender waist). The flower of female palms is delicate, while the flower of male palms is coarse, and likewise the flower of the Barni (a kind of date) is more delicate than the flower of the "al-laun" (the daql, the poorest dates; al-Sihah. Its editor.) So He reminded them of God's blessing in giving them the best and most beneficial palms, because the females bear dates, and Barni is the finest and most excellent of dates. It is also possible that He means their palms enjoyed excellent soil and abundant water and were free from blights, so they bore heavy loads; and when the load is heavy it is "hadim" (bent down), and when it is light it comes out splendid.

It was also said: "hadim" means soft and ripe, as if He said: "and date palms whose fruit has ripened." Al-Hasan recited "watanhituna" with a fatha on the ha'. It was also read "fariheen" and "farihin." Al-farahah means shrewdness and vigor, and from it comes "khayl farihah" (spirited horses). It is used metaphorically for complying with a command and fulfilling it as obedience to the one who commands and is obeyed. Or the command is made obeyed by a legal metaphor, and what is meant is the one who commands, as in their saying: "You have my obedient command," and as in His words, Exalted is He: "And obey my command." If you ask: what is the benefit of His words "and they do not reform"? I say: its benefit is that their corruption is pure corruption with no trace of reform in it, unlike the condition of some corrupters, whose state is mixed with some good.

Al-Shurb: the portion of water, like al-siqy (the watering) and al-qut (the share of sustenance) in the sense of one's allotted portion of the watering. It is also recited with a ḍammah on the shīn (shurb).

It is related that they said: "We want a pregnant she-camel to come out of this rock, which will give birth to a young male camel" (al-saqb: the male offspring of a she-camel, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ). So Ṣāliḥ sat reflecting, and Jibrīl (peace be upon him) said to him: "Pray two rak'ahs and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel emerged, knelt down before them, and gave birth to a young male camel like her in size. It is also reported from Abū Mūsā: "I saw her place of drinking, and it was sixty cubits."

And from Qatādah: "When it was her day of drinking, she drank all of their water, and they had a day of drinking on which she did not drink, [when] the water [was given to them] without harm, by striking or hamstringing or otherwise." The day is described as great because the punishment would descend upon it, and describing the day with this quality is more eloquent than describing the punishment, because when a time is made great by its cause, its effect is all the more severe.

Tafsir (commentary) by al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on surah 26, verses 157–159:

It is related that Mus'ada (Mus'ada ibn Mudrik?) drove her into a narrow pass in a ravine, shot her with an arrow, which struck her leg, and she fell; then Qudar struck her.

It is also related that the one who hamstrung her said: "I will not hamstring her until you all are pleased." So they would enter upon the woman in her curtained chamber and say: "Are you pleased?" She would say: "Yes." And so too their children.

If you ask: Why did the punishment seize them when they had repented? I answer: Their regret was not the regret of penitents; rather it was the regret of those who feared they would be punished with a swift punishment for the hamstringing. It is like one who holds a corrupt opinion about some matter and builds upon it, then regrets and grieves, like the regret of al-Kus'i (al-Kus'i: a clan from Yemen. The Kus'i was a man of theirs who pursued a herd until he took from it a bow, and shot at wild game by night, thinking he had missed; so he broke the bow. When morning came he saw what he had struck of game, and regretted; and the proverb was coined about him by the one who said:

"I regretted the regret of al-Kus'i when
his eyes saw what his hands had done."

Thus it is in al-Sihah. (Editor's note.)), or they regretted the regret of penitents but at the wrong time, namely at the moment of seeing the punishment. God Most High said: "And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds..." (the verse). It was also said: their regret was over having abandoned offspring, but this is far-fetched. The lam in "al-'adhab" (the punishment) is for indicating a punishment of a great day.

If you do not desist from forbidding us and disparaging our affair, you will surely be among those whom we expel from amongst us and drive out of our land. Perhaps those who were expelled used to leave in the worst condition: [[Mahmud said: "i.e., among those whom we expelled. Perhaps they used to leave, those who were expelled, in the worst condition, through being abused and having their possessions confiscated, and similar things." Ahmad said: In the Qur'an, especially in this surah, there often occurs a shift from expressing an act with a verb to expressing it with a derived attributive noun, and then making the one described by it one member of a group. Examples include Pharaoh's words, ﴿I will surely make you one of the imprisoned﴾ (26:29), and their words, ﴿It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers﴾ (26:136), and their words, ﴿You will surely be among those stoned﴾ (26:116), and His words, ﴿I am of those who hate your deed﴾ (26:168). In another place He says, ﴿They were content to be with the women who stay behind﴾ (9:87), and likewise, ﴿Leave us so that we may be with those who sit back﴾. Similar examples are many. The secret of this, and God knows best, is that expressing an act with a verb only conveys that the act occurred. But expressing it with a descriptive noun, and then making the one described by it one member of a group, conveys something beyond the occurrence of the act: that the mentioned attribute is like a mark fixed upon the described person, as if it were a title, and as if he belonged to a group that has become like a specific type known for certain bad marks. Consider this: if you said, "They were content to be left behind," there would be nothing more in that than the report that they stayed behind. Look at the context, His words, ﴿They were content to be with the women who stay behind﴾, and how He attached to them a base title, and made them of a despised, well-known kind marked by the trait of staying behind, until it became a title clinging to them. This answer is general for all such examples that come to you, so reflect on it and appreciate its worth. And God is the Granter of success to what is right."]]. This is also how the rulers behave when they expel someone with whom they are angry, and as the people of Makkah used to treat whoever wanted to emigrate.

Al-Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari, commentary on Surah 26, verses 168–175:

﴿And [he was] among those who detest [it]﴾ is more emphatic than saying ﴿Indeed, I am [one who is] of your deed﴾, just as you say "So-and-so is among the scholars," which is more emphatic than saying "So-and-so is a scholar," because you are testifying that he is counted among their group and that his contribution to them in knowledge is well known. It is also permissible that it means: among the complete ones in your hatred (qalan). Al-qalā is intense hatred, as if it were a hatred that burns the heart and the liver. This indicates the gravity of disobedience. The intended meaning of al-qalā is in terms of religion and piety. The resolve of religion in the religion of God may grow strong until its dislike of sins approaches natural aversion (al-karāhah al-jibilliyyah), ﴿from what they do﴾, that is, from the punishment for their deed, and this is the apparent meaning. It is possible that by al-tanjiyah (deliverance) is meant al-ʿiṣmah (protection).

If you say: what is the meaning of His words ﴿So We delivered him and his family, all of them, except an old woman﴾? I say: its meaning is that He protected him and his family from that, except the old woman, for she was not protected from it, because she was content with it, helped in it, and incited to it (muḥarrishah), and one who is content with disobedience is in the ruling of one who disobeys.

If you say: his family were believers, and had it not been so he would not have asked for their deliverance; so how did you make an exception of the disbelieving one among them?

I say: the exception occurred from "the family," and in this designation she still shares with them by the right of marriage, even though she did not share with them in faith.

If you say: ﴿among those who remain behind﴾ is a qualifier of her, as if it were said: "except an old woman who remained behind," and being one who remained behind was not her attribute at the time of their deliverance?

[Mahmud said: "The prepositional phrase is a qualifier of her, as if it were said: 'except an old woman who remained behind,' and being one who remained behind was not her attribute at the time of their deliverance." I say: its meaning is "except an old woman whose remaining behind is determined," that is, in destruction and punishment.]

Ahmad said: And if you are hasty in lifting the established principle mentioned just now, know that the secret that required turning away from saying, for example, "except an old woman who remained behind," to what is mentioned in the recitation is this: what is mentioned in the recitation requires the attribution of the mark of ruin to her as one of a people marked with this characteristic of destruction, as I have just mentioned. So it is more emphatic than merely describing her with remaining behind. And God knows best.

I say: its meaning is "except an old woman whose remaining behind is determined." And the meaning of "those who remain behind" in punishment and destruction is: those who were not delivered.

It has been said that she was destroyed along with those who went out of the town, by what was rained down upon them of stones. The intended meaning of their destruction (tadmīr) is their total annihilation (al-ightifāk). As for the raining down (al-imṭār), it is from Qatādah: God rained stones from heaven upon the strangers of the people (shudhdhādh al-qawm) and destroyed them. And from Ibn Zayd: He was not satisfied with the overturning until He sent after it a rain of stones.

The subject of ﴿How evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾ (fasā'a maṭaru al-mundharīn) is not intended to refer to specific people; rather, "those who were warned" is a collective noun, and the thing specified by the dispraise is omitted, and it is their rain.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 176–180:

It is recited as "Ashab al-Aykah" with a hamzah and without it, and with a genitive (jarr) on the basis of idafah (annexation), which is the preferred reading. As for one who reads it in the accusative (naṣb) and supposes that Aykah is on the pattern of Laylah, the name of a town, he has been misled by the orthography of the Mushaf, since it is written in this surah and in Surah Sad without an alif. In the Mushaf there are certain words written contrary to the standard rule of the script that has been agreed upon. They were written in these two surahs according to the pronunciation of the reciter, just as grammarians write "lākin" and "lawlā" in this form, to indicate the pronunciation of the abbreviated form, whereas they are written elsewhere in the Qur'an according to the original form, although the story is one and the same. Moreover, Aykah is a name that is not known.

It is related that the People of the Aykah were people of dense trees, and their tree was the doum palm. If you ask: why was it not said, "their brother Shu'ayb," as in the other passages? I say:

They said: Shu'ayb was not from the People of the Aykah. And in a hadith: Shu'ayb, the brother of Madyan, was sent to them and to the People of the Aykah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verse 181–184:

The measuring of quantities falls into three kinds: full, deficient, and excessive. He commanded the obligatory, which is giving full measure (al-iyfa'), and forbade the prohibited, which is cheating in measure (al-tatfif), and He did not mention the excessive. His leaving it out of both the command and the prohibition is evidence that if one does it, he has done good, and if he does not do it, there is no blame on him. It was read as bil-qistas, with the qaf vowelled both with damma and with kasra, and it means the balance (al-mizan). It was also said: al-qirstun. If it derives from al-qist, which is justice, with the ayn doubled, then its pattern is fa'las; otherwise it is quadriliteral. It was also said that it is Roman (Rumiyya) and means justice. One says: "bakhastuhu haqqahu" (I diminished his right), meaning I reduced it for him. From this comes the term al-maks (the tax on sales) being called al-bakhs. It is general in every right established for someone, that it must not be encroached upon, and in every property, that its owner must not be deprived of it or have it reduced, and that it must not be disposed of except with his permission in a lawful manner. One says: "tha'a fi al-ard," "tha'a," and "'a'a," and that is like highway robbery, raiding, and the destruction of crops, and they used to do that along with their assumption of various kinds of corruption, so they were forbidden from that. It was also read as al-jibilla, on the pattern of al-ublla. And al-jibilla, on the pattern of al-khilqa, [[The author's words "al-ublla wa-al-jibilla": in al-Sihah, "al-ublla" with damma and a doubled lam means a piece of dates ("al-ghadra" from dates). And in it: "al-ghadra" is a piece of meat when it is gathered together. And also in it: al-jibilla is creation (al-khilqa). From it is His saying, Exalted is He: "wa-al-jibilata al-awwalin" (and the earlier generations), and al-Hasan read it with damma. (Ibn Atiyya? marked (ع))]].

Their meaning is one: that is, "dhawi al-jibilla" (those who possess the created nature), and it is like your saying "wa-al-khalqa al-awwalin" (and the earlier creation).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verse 185–186:

If you ask: Does the meaning differ by inserting the waw here and omitting it in the story of Thamud? I answer: When the waw is inserted, two meanings are intended, both of which are, in their view, incompatible with prophethood: being bewitched (tasḥīr) and being human (bashariyya). That is, the Messenger cannot be one who is bewitched, and he cannot be a human being. When the waw is omitted, only one meaning is intended, namely that he is bewitched, and then they affirm that he is a human being like them.

If you ask: How do the light (mukhaffafa) form of inna and its lam separate between the verb of opinion (fi'l al-zann) and its second object? I answer: Their original arrangement is that they separate between the subject and the predicate, as when you say: inna Zaydan la-munṭaliq ("indeed Zayd is certainly departing"). Since the two chapters, namely the chapter of kana and the chapter of ẓanantu, are of the same kind as the chapter of the subject and predicate, this was applied to both chapters, so it is said: in kana Zaydun la-munṭaliqan, and in ẓanantuhu la-munṭaliqan.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verse 187:

It is read as "kisafan" (kisafan), both with a sukun and with a harakah (vowel), and both are plurals of "kisfah" (kisfah), like "qita'" and "sidr." It was also said: "al-kisf" and "al-kisfah" are like "al-ri'" and "al-ri'ah," and it means a piece. "Kasafahu" means he cut it. "Al-sama'" means the clouds, or the canopy.

Their asking for that was only due to their determination in denial and rejection. Had there been even the slightest inclination in them towards belief, they would not have entertained it in their minds, let alone requested it. The meaning is: if you are truthful that you are a prophet, then call upon God to make pieces of the sky fall upon us.

My Lord is most knowing of what you do. He means: God is most knowing of your deeds and of the punishment you deserve for them. If He wills to punish you by dropping fragments from the sky, He does so; and if He wills some other punishment, then judgment and will belong to Him.

So God seized them in the manner they had asked for, the punishment of the shade-cloud, if by "the sky" they meant the cloud. If by "the shade" they meant something that shades, then God turned their request away from them. It is related that He withheld the wind from them for seven days and let loose upon them al-wamad [[Its meaning is the intense heat of the night, as in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]], so that it took their breaths. Neither shade, nor water, nor any cave-hollow benefited them. They were compelled to go out into the open desert, and a cloud overshadowed them. They found in it coolness and a gentle breeze, so they gathered beneath it, and it rained fire upon them, and they were burned.

It is also related that Shuʿayb was sent to two communities: the people of Madyan and the people of al-Aykah. The people of Madyan were destroyed by the Cry (ṣayḥa) of Jibril, and the people of al-Aykah by the punishment of the Day of the Shade.

If you ask: how did [the Qur'an] repeat in this surah, at the beginning and at the end of each story, what it repeated? I say: each story in it is like a revelation in its own right, and it contains the same lessons as the others. So each one deserved to open with what its companion opened with, and to close with what its companion closed with. Moreover, repetition establishes meanings in the souls and fixes them in the breasts. Do you not see that there is no way to retain knowledge except by repeating what one wishes to retain? The more it is repeated, the more firmly it settles in the heart, the deeper it takes root in understanding, the more securely it is kept in memory, and the further it is from being forgotten. Also, these stories have struck ears that are deaf to listening to the truth, and hearts that are sealed against reflecting upon it. So they were reinforced with admonition and reminder, and reiterated with repetition and recurrence, perhaps that this might open an ear, or split open a mind, or polish an intellect whose polishing has long been neglected, or clear an understanding that the accumulation of rust has covered.

Or it may be connected to *nazala* (sent down), in which case the meaning is: He sent it down in the Arabic tongue.

If he is addressed in another language, even if he is skilled in it, his attention is first on its words and then on their meanings. This establishes that it was sent down upon his heart by its descent in a clear Arabic tongue.

Or it may be connected to *nazala* (sent down), in which case the meaning is: He sent it down in the Arabic tongue.

[[He (al-Zamakhshari) finished his words. He said: Know that the earlier verses are as preliminaries to these verses, for God has made clear that He sent it down in their language, which they know no other than, and in a clear Arabic tongue; so if any part of it were difficult for them to understand, the explanation would be readily at hand with Him. Whereas if He had sent it down in a non-Arabic tongue, they might make the excuse that they cannot understand what is obscure to their minds of its meanings. So He has removed their excuses and refuted their arguments, and has made it enter their hearts and has enabled them to understand it to the utmost degree. But He did not grant them success; rather He decreed upon them that they would not believe. Ahmad said: By His saying "decreed upon them that they would not believe" He means "knew that they would not believe," because *al-taqdir* (decree) in His view is knowledge. The truth is that God willed from them that they would not believe. This is a confirmation of the answer to an assumed question, namely that it might be said: their hearts are far from accepting the truth, and it does not enter them in any way or by any means, so how can the truth penetrate them? It is answered with this reply, and God knows best.]] So that you may warn by it, because if He had sent it down in a non-Arabic tongue they would have turned away from it entirely and said: "What are we to do with what we do not understand?" and warning by it would have been impossible. In this view, the fact that its sending down is in Arabic, which is your tongue and the tongue of your people, is a sending down upon your heart, because you understand it and your people understand it. Had it been non-Arabic, it would have descended upon your hearing rather than your heart, because you would hear the sounds of letters whose meanings you do not understand or grasp. A person may know several languages; but when he is addressed in the language he was first taught, grew up upon and was molded by, his heart is directed only to the meanings of the speech, which he receives with his heart, and he hardly notices how the words were put together. If he is addressed in another language, even if he is skilled in it, his attention is first on its words and then on their meanings. This establishes that it was sent down upon his heart by its descent in a clear Arabic tongue.

Also read: yakun (with the masculine verb form). Āyatun is in the accusative as its predicate, and an-ya'lamahu is the subject. Another reading is also transmitted: takun (with the feminine verb form), in which āyatan is the subject and an-ya'lamahu is the predicate. This is not like the first reading, because an indefinite noun is then the subject and a definite phrase the predicate. Another explanation has been offered to avoid this problem: the pronoun in yakun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa), and āyatan an-ya'lamahu is a clause standing in the position of the predicate. It is also permitted on this view that lahum āyatun be the clause of the matter (jumlat al-sha'n), with an-ya'lamahu in apposition (badal) to āyatun. It is also permitted, with the accusative of āyatan, to feminize yakun, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then their trial was not but that they said﴾ [6:23]. From this is the verse of Labid: "So he went forward and advanced it, and his habit was, when its feet turned back, ..." [[The explanation of this witness was given earlier in this part, page 13; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

Also read: ta'lamahu (with the letter tā'). The "scholars of the Children of Israel" (ʿulamā' Banī Isrā'īl) are ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and others. God Almighty said: ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say: "We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed we were Muslims before it."﴾ [28:53]. If you ask: how was "ʿulamāʾ" written in the muṣḥaf with a wāw before the alif? I answer: it was written according to the dialect of those who incline the alif toward the wāw, and on this dialect the words "al-ṣalawāt," "al-zakāt," and "al-ribā" were written.

Al-A'jam: the one who cannot express himself clearly, in whose tongue there is a foreignness and inarticulateness. Al-a'jamī is similar to it, except that the added yā' of relation (ya' al-nisba) adds emphasis. Al-Ḥasan recited al-a'jamīyīn. Since whoever speaks in a language other than theirs, they do not comprehend his speech, they called him a'jam and a'jamī, likening him to one who does not express himself clearly or make himself understood. And they called every creature with a voice among the beasts, birds and others a'jam. Ḥumayd said:

"And no Arab whose heart was stirred by a foreign voice [a'jam]. It was nothing but a dove that stirred this longing in me, calling to her mate, the male with a young one, lamenting and grieving..."

"So she sang upon a branch at evening, and left no mourning woman in her lament without grief..."

"I marvel how her song can be clear and eloquent, yet she opens her mouth not with speech..."

"And no one like me was stirred by the voice of a creature like her, nor an Arab stirred by a foreign voice [a'jam]."

These are by Ḥumayd ibn Thawr, when his beloved Salmā had departed, and he says: what stirred this longing and roused it, so that it blazed in my heart, was nothing but a dove calling her mate and a young one. Sāq ḥurr is an idafa compound, meaning the male of the turtle-dove, or the male pigeon in general. Al-ḥurr (with a ḍamma) is the chick of the dove. Al-tarḥa is sorrow, the opposite of joy; al-tanaddum is regret over what has passed. It is also narrated as "tarannum," meaning beautifying the voice. Both are in the accusative as circumstantial states (ḥāl): i.e., sorrowful and regretful, or possessing sorrow and regret. ʿAshiyy is in the accusative as an adverb of time. "Fa-lam tadaʿ": i.e., she leaves a mourning woman in her singing without regret [mutanaddiman]: i.e., regret, or something by which one regrets or in which one regrets. It is permissible that the pronoun in "nawḥihā" refers to the mourning woman, and "annā" means "how" or "from where," and the interrogation is one of wonder. Al-faṣīḥ is the clear one, free of accent and convolution. "Faghara fāhu yafghuruhu," from the pattern of nafaʿa, means he opened it, i.e., while she did not open her mouth in speech, but her voice comes out from her chest. "Shāqahu" means he caused him longing, and al-ʿarabī is the one who expresses himself clearly. Al-aʿjam is the one among animals who does not express himself clearly; the Arabs transferred it to those whose speech they do not understand and whose meaning they do not grasp, and they sometimes attached the nisba yā' to it for intensifying the extremity of foreignness. Between it and ʿarabī there is antithetical contrast (ṭibāq al-taḍādd).

"Salaknāhu" means: We caused it to enter, and We established it. The meaning is: We sent down this Qur'an upon an Arab man in a clear Arabic tongue; they heard it, understood it, recognized its eloquence, and that it is inimitable and cannot be opposed by speech like it. To this is added the agreement of the scholars of the earlier revealed books that the good tidings of its descent, and the description of the one upon whom it was sent and his attributes, were in their books, and its meanings and narratives were contained in them. Thereby it is established that it is from God and not fables, as they claimed. Yet they did not believe in it and denied it, and at times called it poetry, and at other times sorcery, and they said: it is a fabrication of Muḥammad and his invention. "And had We sent it down upon some of the foreigners who do not speak Arabic well, let alone being able to compose its like, and he recited it to them thus, eloquent and inimitable, challenging them with it, they would have disbelieved in it as they disbelieved, and they would have invented an excuse for their denial, and they would have called it sorcery." Then He said: "Thus We caused it to enter": that is, in the same manner We caused it to enter into their hearts; in this way We established it and fixed it therein, and upon this state and this attribute of disbelief in it and denial of it We placed it in them. However He deals with them and acts toward them, and in whatever manner He arranges their affair, there is no way for them to change from their denial and rejection of it, as He said: "And if We had sent down to you a book on paper, and they touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, 'This is nothing but manifest sorcery.'"

If you say: How is "salaka" with the attribute of denial ascribed to His essence? I say: it is intended to show that its firmness as denial is established in their hearts in the strongest firmness, and He affirmed it, making it like a matter they were fashioned upon and created with. Do you not see their saying: "He is naturally disposed to stinginess," meaning that stinginess is firmly rooted in him, because innate matters are more established than accidental ones? The proof of this is that He ascribed the abandonment of belief in it to them after it, in His words: "they do not believe in it."

If you say: What is the position of "lā yu'minūna bihi" from His words "We caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals"? I say: its position relative to it is that of the place and the summary, because it is brought to affirm that it is firmly fixed in their hearts as denied and rejected, so it follows what establishes this meaning, namely that they continue in denial of it and rejection of it until they witness the threat. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial state: i.e., We caused it to enter into them not believing in it.

Al-Ḥasan recited "fa-ta'tīhim" with the tā' (feminine), meaning the Hour. "Baghtatan" with a vowel on the ghayn. In the reading of Ubayy: "wa-yarawhu baghtatan" (and they will see it suddenly).

If you say: What is the meaning of the sequence (ta'qīb) in His words "fa-ya'tiyahum baghtatan... fa-yaqūlū"? I say: the meaning is not that the seeing of the punishment, its sudden arrival, and the request for respite occur one right after another in time; rather, the meaning is their ordering in severity, as if it were said: they do not believe in the Qur'an until their seeing of the punishment, which is more severe than that, and its reaching them suddenly, which is more severe than that, and which is their request for respite. An example of this is that you say to one you are admonishing: "If the righteous despise you, then God despises you," for you do not mean by this ordering that God's contempt occurs immediately after the contempt of the righteous, but rather you intend to order the severity of the matter upon the wrongdoer, and that there results for him from his wrongdoing the contempt of the righteous, and what is more severe than their contempt: the contempt of God. This structure is used, and in its place comes:

"Will they then seek to hasten Our punishment?" This is a rebuke to them with denial and mockery. Its meaning: how can one seek to hasten the punishment who is exposed to a punishment in which he asks for the kind of respite and delay he is now in, for even a moment, and is not granted it? It is possible that this is a narration of a reproach with which they will be rebuked when they seek respite on that day; and "yasta'jilūna" in this sense is a narration of a past state. There is another aspect connected to what follows: their hastening for the punishment was only because they believed it would not occur or befall them, and that they would be enjoying long lives in safety and security. So He, exalted is He, said: "Will they then seek to hasten Our punishment?" in insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope. Then He said: "Suppose that the matter is as they believe of their being given enjoyment and long life; then when the threat reaches them after that, what will the long past of their lives and the goodness of their livelihoods avail them then?"

It is reported from Maymūn ibn Mihrān that he met al-Ḥasan during the circumambulation, and he had been wishing to meet him. He said to him: "Admonish me." Al-Ḥasan did not add to it beyond reciting this verse. Maymūn said: "You have admonished and made it complete." It is also recited "yumta'ūn" with the lightened form.

There is another aspect connected to what follows: their hastening for the punishment was only because they believed it would not occur or befall them, and that they would be enjoying long lives in safety and security. So He, exalted is He, said: "Will they then seek to hasten Our punishment?" in insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope. Then He said: "Suppose that the matter is as they believe of their being given enjoyment and long life; then when the threat reaches them after that, what will the long past of their lives and the goodness of their livelihoods avail them then?"

It is reported from Maymūn ibn Mihrān that he met al-Ḥasan during the circumambulation, and he had been wishing to meet him. He said to him: "Admonish me." Al-Ḥasan did not add to it beyond reciting this verse. Maymūn said: "You have admonished and made it complete." It is also recited "yumta'ūn" with the lightened form.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 208–209:

Mundhirun (warners): messengers who warn them. Dhikra (as a reminder), in the accusative, meaning tadhkira (admonition). This may be because "andhara" and "dhakara" are close in meaning, so it is as if it were said: "mudhakkirun tadhkira" (they remind with a reminder). Or it is because it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in mundhirun, meaning: they warn them while possessing admonition (dhawi tadhkira). Or it is because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), in the sense that they warn for the sake of exhortation and reminder. Or it is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "this is a reminder" (hadhihi dhikra), and the sentence is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya). Or it is a qualifier (sifa), meaning: "warners who possess a reminder" (mundhirun dhawu dhikra). Or they made it dhikra because of their thoroughness in reminding and their extensiveness in it (li-imANihim fi al-tadhkira wa-itnabihim fihā).

Another aspect: that dhikra is related to ahlakna (We destroyed) as an object of purpose. The meaning: "We did not destroy any town's people, being wrongdoers, except after We had established the proof against them by sending warners to them, so that their destruction would be a reminder and a lesson to others, so that they would not disobey as they disobeyed. Nor were We wrongdoers, so as to destroy a people who were not wrongdoers." This aspect is the one relied upon.

If you ask: how is the waw (wa) detached from the clause after "illa" (except), while it was not detached from it in His saying: "And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree (wa-la-ha kitabun ma'lum)"? I answer: the original is that the waw is detached, because the clause is a qualifier of "qarya" (town). When the waw is added, it is for emphasizing the joining of the qualifier to the qualified, as in His saying: "seven, and their eighth is their dog" (sab'atun wa-thaminuhum kalbuhum).

They used to say: Muhammad is a soothsayer (kahin), and what descends upon him is of the same kind as what the devils (shayatin) bring down upon the soothsayers. But God refuted them, saying that this is not something the devils can easily accomplish or are able to do, because they are pelted with shooting stars and kept away from listening to the speech of the inhabitants of heaven. Al-Hasan read: "al-shayatun." Its basis is that he saw its ending as like the ending of Yabrin and Filastin, so he had the choice between inflecting the nun as a case-ending (i'rab) and inflecting it as the letters before it, so he would say al-shayatin and al-shayatun, just as the Arabs had the choice between saying yabrun and yabrin, and filastun and filastin.

Its proper derivation is from al-shaytuwa, which means destruction, just as falsehood (al-batil) is called that. From al-Farra': "The Shaykh (al-Hasan) erred in his reading 'al-shayatun'; he thought it was the nun that has two spellings." Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "If it is permissible to cite the speech of al-'Ajjaj and Ru'ba as evidence, then why is it not permissible to cite the speech of al-Hasan and his companion, meaning Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqi'? Yet we know that the two of them did not recite it this way except after having heard it."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 213–214:

He knew that this would not happen, but He intended by it to stir him to increase in sincerity and piety. And in it there is grace (lutf) for all the obligated persons (mukallafun), as He said: ﴿And if he had invented against Us some sayings﴾ [69:44–45]. As for ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾ [10:94], there are two aspects. The first: that he be commanded to warn the nearest of his people, then the next nearest, beginning in this with the one most deserving of beginning, and then with the one after him, and that he give priority to warning them over warning others, as was related from him, peace be upon him:

That when he entered Mecca he said: "Every usury (riba) of the Jahiliyyah is abolished under these two feet of mine, and the first usury I abolish is the usury of al-'Abbas" [[Muslim narrated it from the lengthy hadith of Jabir on the description of the Hajj, and al-Tibi attributed it to al-Tirmidhi from the narration of 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas, though it is not in his complete form.]].

The second: that he be commanded not to let him be moved by the tenderness and compassion that a relative feels for a relative, and not to show them favoritism in warning and threatening. It is related that when it was revealed, he climbed al-Safa and called out, "The nearest, then the nearest, clan by clan," and said: "O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib! O sons of Hashim! O sons of 'Abd Manaf! O 'Abbas, uncle of the Prophet! O Safiyya, aunt of the Messenger of Allah! Indeed I cannot avail you anything against Allah; ask me of my wealth whatever you wish" [[Ibn Hibban narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood when ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ was revealed and said: 'O sons of 'Abd Manaf, O sons of Hashim, I cannot avail you anything against Allah.' Muslim narrated from the hadith of 'A'ishah: 'When ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood upon al-Safa and said: "O Fatimah daughter of Muhammad, O Safiyya daughter of 'Abd al-Muttalib, O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib: I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Ask me of my wealth whatever you wish."' Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Abu Umamah, who said: "When ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out and said: 'O sons of Hashim, buy yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot avail you anything against Allah. O 'A'ishah daughter of Abu Bakr, O Hafsah daughter of 'Umar, O Umm Salamah, O Fatimah daughter of Muhammad, O Umm al-Zubayr, aunt of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: buy yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot avail you anything against Allah.'"]].

It is also related that he gathered the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, and they were forty men at that time. Each man of them would eat a whole young camel and drink a great bowl (al-'us) [[His saying "and drink the 'us" is the great cup, as in al-Sihah.]] with a sheep's leg and a bowl of milk. They ate and drank until they had had their fill, and then he warned them and said:

"O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, if I told you that there were horses at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said:

"Then indeed I am a warner to you before a severe punishment."

It is also related that he said: "O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, O sons of Hashim, O sons of 'Abd Manaf, ransom yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot avail you anything." Then he said: "O 'A'ishah daughter of Abu Bakr, O Hafsah daughter of 'Umar, O Fatimah daughter of Muhammad, O Safiyya aunt of Muhammad, ransom yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot avail you anything."

[[As for its beginning, Ibn Ishaq narrated it in al-Maghazi, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il through his chain, from Ibn 'Abbas at length.

Al-Bazzar and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il narrated through 'Abbad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Asadi, from 'Ali, who said: "When ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'Prepare for me a sheep's leg with a sa' of food, and prepare a bowl of milk.' I did so. Then he said to me: 'Gather for me the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib.' I gathered them, and they were forty men at that time. I placed the food before them, and they ate until they were satisfied, and among them were those who would eat a young camel and drink a great bowl. Then I brought the bowl and they drank until they were quenched."

As for the rest of it, it is agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out until he ascended al-Safa and called out: 'Ya sabahah!' So they gathered to him, and he said: 'O sons of 'Abd Manaf, O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, if I told you that horsemen were coming out at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?' They said: 'We have never found you to be a liar.' He said: 'Then indeed I am a warner to you before a severe punishment.' Abu Lahab said: 'Ruin to you! Is it for this that you gathered us?' Then this surah was revealed: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he﴾ [111:1]."]].

The bird, when it wants to descend to alight, lowers its wing and droops it, and when it wants to rise to fly, it raises its wing. So lowering the wing at the time of descent was made a metaphor for humility and gentleness of manner. From this is the saying of one of them:

"You are renowned for lowering the wing... so do not be, in raising it, a falcon."

[[It likens him to a bird that is tender toward its young and lowers its wing to them out of mercy, so the lowering of the wing is borrowed for that by way of tamthil (metaphorical representation), and it is accompanied by his saying "so do not be, in raising it, a falcon", meaning resembling the falcon (ajdal), which is the hawk in harshness and roughness, or in arrogance and haughtiness. It is also permissible that lowering the wing is a kinaya (allusion) for what it entails of tenderness, mercy and gentleness, and raising it is a kinaya for harshness and roughness; and between lowering and raising there is tibaq (antithesis) of opposition.]]

He forbids him from arrogance after humility. If you say: "Those who follow the Messenger are the believers, and the believers are those who follow the Messenger, so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿to those who follow you of the believers﴾?" I say: there are two aspects. One is that He calls them believers before they have entered faith, because they are approaching it. The other is that by "the believers" He means those who affirm with their tongues, and they are of two types: a type that affirmed and followed the Messenger of Allah in what he brought, and a type from whom nothing was found but mere affirmation, and then they are either hypocrites or wrongdoers (fasiqun), and the hypocrite and the wrongdoer are not to be shown lowering of the wing. The meaning is: of the believers, of your kin and others; that is, warn your people, and if they follow you and obey you, then lower your wing to them, and if they disobey you and do not follow you, then disassociate yourself from them and from their deeds, from associating partners with Allah and others.

And put your trust in Allah, and He will suffice you against the evil of those who disobey you, among them and among others. Tawakkul (reliance, trusting) means a man entrusting his affair to the One who holds his affair and is able to benefit or harm him. They said: the one who relies upon Allah is he who, when a matter befalls him, does not try to repel it from himself by means that are disobedience to Allah. Accordingly, if a person falls into a trial and then asks another for his deliverance, he has not left the bounds of tawakkul, because he has not tried to repel what has come upon him by disobeying Allah.

In the codices of the people of Madina and Syria it reads: "fa-tawakkal" (so trust), and Nafi' and Ibn Amir recited it thus. It has two interpretations in terms of coordination: that it is coordinated with "fa-qul" (so say), or with "fa-la tad'u" (so do not call upon). ﴿Upon the Mighty, the Merciful﴾: upon the One who subdues your enemies by His might and grants you victory over them by His mercy.

Then he follows his being merciful toward His Messenger with something that is among the causes of mercy: namely, mentioning what he used to do in the depths of the night, standing in prayer for tahajjud (night worship), and turning about to observe the condition of the worshippers among his Companions, so that he might see them without their noticing, and inwardly know the secret of their affairs, how they worship Allah and how they labour for their Hereafter. It is related that when the obligation of qiyam al-layl (night prayer) was abrogated (naskh), he went around the houses of his Companions that night to see what they were doing, out of his eagerness for them and for the good deeds and abundant rewards that were found among them. He found their houses like beehives (buzzing), because of the sound of their murmuring with the remembrance of Allah and recitation. By "the worshippers" (al-sajidin) is meant those who pray. It has also been said that the meaning is: He sees you when you stand to lead the people in congregational prayer. ﴿And your turning among the worshippers﴾: His directing of you among them through your standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting when you lead them.

It is reported from Muqatil that he asked Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, "Do you find congregational prayer in the Qur'an?" He said, "It does not come to my mind." So he recited to him this verse.

It may also mean: your condition is not hidden from Him whenever you stand and turn among the worshippers in the management of the affairs of religion. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, of what you say, the All-Knowing, of what you intend and do.﴾

It has also been said: it is the turning of His sight over those who pray behind you, from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Complete the bowing and prostration, for by Allah, I see you from behind my back when you bow and prostrate." [Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Qatada from Anas, with this meaning. The wording mentioned is in al-Nasa'i, and they both agreed upon it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra with the wording: "Do you see my qibla here? By Allah, your bowing and your prostration are not hidden from me, and I see you from behind my back."]

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 26, verses 221–222:**

Before they were barred by being pelted with meteors, they used to listen to the Highest Assembly (*al-mala' al-a'la*), snatching some of what they said from the unseen matters they had learned, and then they would convey it to their associates among those men. ﴿وَأَكْثَرُهُمْ كاذِبُونَ﴾ in what they convey to them, because they tell them what they did not hear. It is also said: ﴿يُلْقُونَ السَّمْعَ﴾ means they convey to their associates the heard [matter], i.e., what was heard from the angels. It is also said: the liars cast their hearing toward the devils, so they receive their revelation from them; or they convey what they heard from the devils to people. ﴿وَأَكْثَرُ الْأَفَّاكِينَ كاذِبُونَ﴾ attribute to the devils what the devils never revealed to them, and you will find that most of what they judge is falsehood and lies.

If you ask: how does the preposition (*harf al-jarr*) enter upon ﴿مَنْ﴾, which implies the meaning of interrogation, when interrogation has the foremost place in the sentence (*sadr al-kalam*)? Do you not see your saying: *a-'alā Zaydin marartu?* (Was it over Zayd that I passed?), and you do not say: *'alā a-Zaydun marartu?* I say: the implication of the expression does not mean that the noun indicates two meanings together, the meaning of the noun and the meaning of the particle. Rather, its meaning is that the original form was *a-min*, so the interrogative particle (*harf al-istifham*) was deleted and the usage continued with its deletion, just as it was deleted from *hal*, whose original form was *ahal*. [The poet] said:

*"Ahl ra'ūnā bi-safḥi l-qā'i dhī l-akami"* (Did they see us at the wide plain with its hills?)

When you insert the preposition upon ﴿مَنْ﴾, imagine the hamza placed before the preposition in your mind, as if you are saying: *a-'alā man tanazzalu l-shayāṭīn* (Over whom do the devils descend?), like your saying: *a-'alā Zaydin marartu?*

It may be in the genitive position as a qualifier of ﴿كُلِّ أَفَّاكٍ﴾, because it has the sense of the plural. It may also have no position, being a new (resumed) sentence, as if someone asked: "What happens to the liars?" and it was answered: "They do such-and-such."

If you ask: how is it said ﴿وَأَكْثَرُهُمْ كاذِبُونَ﴾ after it was already decided that each of them is a liar? I say: the liars are those who abound in lying, and that does not indicate that they speak only lies. So the meaning is that few of these liars speak truthfully about what is related from the jinn, and most of them fabricate against him.

If you ask: ﴿وَإِنَّهُ لَتَنْزِيلُ رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ * وَما تَنَزَّلَتْ بِهِ الشَّياطِينُ * هَلْ أُنَبِّئُكُمْ عَلى مَنْ تَنَزَّلُ الشَّياطِينُ﴾, why did He separate them, while they are sisters? I say: He intended to separate them with verses that do not share their meaning, in order to return to the mention of them and to renew the mention of what is in them again and again. Thereby it indicates that the meaning in which they were sent down is among the meanings whose opposite Allah greatly detests. An example of this is a man who speaks of a matter while his heart is preoccupied with some part of it and has excessive concern for it, so you see him repeat its mention and never cease returning to it.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, commentary on Surah 26, verses 225–226:

Such things are not admired from them, nor are they moved by their words, except by the erring (al-ghawun), the foolish (al-sufaha') and the rogues (al-shuttar). It is also said: al-ghawun are the reciters of poetry (al-rawun). It is also said: they are the devils. It is also said: they are the poets of Quraysh: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara, Hubayra ibn Abi Wahb al-Makhzumi, Musafi' ibn 'Abd Manaf, and Abu 'Izza al-Jumahi; and from Thaqif: Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. They said: 'We say the same as the words of Muhammad', and they used to satirise him, and Bedouins of their people would gather to them, listening to their poems and their satires. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "wa-al-shu'ara'" in the accusative (al-nasb), by suppressing a verb which the apparent one explains. Abu 'Ubayd said: the thing that predominated over him was the love of the accusative, and he recited: "hammalata al-hatab" (the carrier of firewood), "wa-al-sariqu wa-al-sariqa" (the thief, male and female), and "surat-un anzalnaha" (a surah which We sent down)."

"Another reading is 'yattabi'uhum', with the lightening (al-takhfif). And 'yatba'uhum', with a sukun on the ayn, likening it to 'ba'du' with 'adud'."

"Mention of the valley and the wandering (al-hayum): in it is an image of their going off into every path of speech, their deviation and lack of concern with falsehood in speech, and their transgression of the bounds of moderation in it, such that they prefer the most cowardly of people over 'Antara, the stingiest over Hatim, and that they accuse the innocent (yabhatu al-bari') and call the pious corrupt (yafsiqu al-taqi)."

*Fa-batna bi-janibay musarra'at... wa-bittu afuddu aghlaqa al-khitami*
